Benchmark.title: CIS Everpure FlashArray Purity 6.9.x Benchmark
Benchmark.description: All CIS Benchmarks ™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to maintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be used in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: • Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and quickly updating with the latest security patches. • End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), etc.). • Logging and monitoring user and system activity. In the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity program. Important Usage Information All Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They can be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of manual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with assessment: • CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT ® Pro Assessor) • CIS Benchmarks ™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling These tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of systems and applications. NOTE: Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can be fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL Recommendations ( Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are important for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for audits. Key Stakeholders Cybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative within an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and efficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration guidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions to specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the problematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. These exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing purposes. Apply the Correct Version of a Benchmark Benchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and applying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to be incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target systems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed: • Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the environment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of Benchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and Stand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. Applying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. • Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, but especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently and using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for auditing and remediation. Exceptions The guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not requirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The Benchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, with known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the Impact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific requirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a Recommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend that a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system's primary purpose is to function as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this Recommendation for that specific server). In the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and acceptable, and should be handled as follows: • The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well documented for audit purposes. • A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the future, if applicable. • If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward mitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. It is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and which settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for the organization. Remediation CIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of hardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark's “Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make that Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. When remediating systems (changing configuration settings on deployed systems as per the Benchmark's Recommendations), please approach this with caution and test thoroughly. The following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: • CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be applied to production systems without proper testing. • Proper testing consists of the following: o Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted systems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations (e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). o Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if there might be an issue with the targeted systems. o Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues arise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production systems. o When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production systems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be resolved prior to deploying more broadly. o When the initial deployment above is completed successfully, iteratively deploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this process until the full deployment is complete. Summary Using the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being selective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible to harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe manner. NOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks ™ are available for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats of the CIS Benchmarks ™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for CIS SecureSuite ® members. CIS-CAT ® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite ® members. Target Technology Details This document provides prescriptive guidance for establishing a secure configuration posture for Everpure FlashArray systems running Purity version 6.9.x. The guidance broadly assumes that operations are being performed by an administrator with appropriate privileges. Operations performed without sufficient permissions may produce unexpected results or fail to make the intended changes to the system. Certain configuration guidance within this document may necessitate contacting Everpure Support at support@everpuredata.com. For inquiries, commentary, or suggestions regarding enhancements to this guide, please direct correspondence to feedback@cisecurity.org.

Rule.title: Ensure a management SAML SSO configuration is created and enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Purity can be integrated with an external identity provider (IDP) that supports SAML.
This allows for single-sign-on (SSO) functionality in the Everpure Web UI, with user provisioning, authentication, and authorization being controlled by the IDP.
Everpure recommends that you create and enable a management SAML configuration.

Rationale:
SAML provides mechanisms for more secure authentication to FlashArray. IDPs can provide assertions about user information, which are digitally signed, allowing FlashArray, acting as the Service Provider (SP), to gather user details in a trusted manner for user authentication and authorization.
This allows authentication to be centralized with an IDP, allowing for the IDP to enforce strong central controls, such as multi-factor authentication, device trust mechanisms, and other security capabilities provided by your IDP.
IDPs can directly provide user authorization information to Purity systems using a custom "purity_roles" SAML claim. Alternatively, the array can be configured to map authorization information based on groups, allowing a standard SAML group to be used.
In either case, it puts the IDP in control of information used to authorize users.
IDP assertions can be optionally encrypted, and FlashArray's authentication assertions can be optionally signed as well, providing additional security controls that may be valuable depending on your environment.
Users who have logged into the Web UI using SAML may also login via SSH using a public key or SSH certificate, and may login via the REST API with an API Token or OAuth JWT, but their authorization must be periodically refreshed via SAML login.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure the array as a Service Provider (SP), exchange metadata or certificates with your Identity Provider, and rigorously test the configuration before enabling SSO.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies and scroll to the SAML2 SSO pane.
• Click the + (Create SAML2 SSO) icon.
• In the Name field, enter a local display name for the SAML2 SSO configuration.
• In the Array URL field, enter the FlashArray URL using HTTPS.
• Enter either the IdP Metadata URL, or manually enter the IdP Entity ID, IdP URL, and click Edit next to Verification Certificate to paste your IdP's PEM- formatted token-signing certificate.
• Click Test at the bottom of the window to run a basic configuration test, then click Save.
• From the SAML2 SSO pane, click Test and then E2E Test to run the mandatory End-to-End test, which will redirect you to sign in with your IdP credentials.
• Warning: Only proceed if the End-to-End test successfully passes, otherwise all array users could be locked out of the GUI.
• Click the Configuration edit icon, slide the Enabled toggle to the right (blue), and click Save.
From the CLI:
• Create the SAML provider: Create the configuration using the puresso saml2 create command. You can use an IdP metadata XML file or manually specify the URLs.
• Command Syntax (Metadata): puresso saml2 create --array-url <ARRAY_URL> --idp-metadata-url <IDP_METADATA_URL> <IDP_NAME>.
• Command Syntax (Manual): puresso saml2 create --array-url <ARRAY_URL> --idp-entity-id <IDP_ENTITY_ID> --idp-url <IDP_URL> - -verification-certificate <IDP_NAME>. (Note: Purity will prompt interactively for the PEM-formatted verification certificate if the flag is used).
• Test the configuration: Run the puresso saml2 test command to verify the array URL, IdP connectivity, and certificate correctness.
• Enable SAML2 SSO: Once testing passes, enable the configuration.
• Command Syntax: puresso saml2 enable <IDP_NAME>.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least one SAML Identity Provider (IdP) is configured, its status is actively enabled, it references the correct IdP URL and verification certificate, and that the configuration successfully passes diagnostic connectivity tests.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies and scroll to the SAML2 SSO pane.
• Verify that the Enabled status is set to true.
• Review the configured settings (such as Array URL, IdP URL, and Metadata URL) to confirm they reference the correct Identity Provider.
• Test the configuration: Click Test to open the Test SAML2 SSO Configuration dialog, review the basic test results, and then click E2E Test to run the End-to- End test. Verify that the authentication process successfully redirects and returns a Passed status without errors.
From the CLI:
• Run the command puresso saml2 list to display configured SAML providers.
• Review the output to confirm that a SAML provider is present and its enabled status is True.
• Run the command puresso saml2 list --verification-certificate to view the full verification certificate details and verify the certificate issuer and expiry date.
• Test the configuration: Run the command puresso saml2 test [IDP-NAME] to verify the array URL correctness, IdP connectivity, directory service correctness, and verification certificate validity.

Rule.title: Ensure a management LDAP/Active Directory service is configured and enabled with at least one group mapped
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If your environment does not support SAML, Purity can be integrated with an external identity provider (IDP) that supports LDAP. This allows for password login functionality in the Everpure Web UI and CLI, with user provisioning, password management, and authorization being controlled by the IDP.
If a SAML configuration does not exist, Everpure recommends that you configure and enable the management LDAP directory service, with at least 1 group granted access to the array.

Rationale:
FlashArray can be configured to communicate with one or more LDAP servers using the LDAP protocol and a service account.
This LDAP communication channel is used to verify user passwords during password- based login, and retrieve information on the groups to which a user belongs for authorization purposes.
This allows account management, authorization information, and passwords to be centralized within an IDP, allowing for the IDP to provision, de-provision, authorize, and de-authorize accounts centrally.
An array can be configured to map authorization information based on directory server groups, and a user will be granted the combination of all roles mapped to groups to which they belong. Nested groups are also supported.
Users who are authorized via LDAP may also login via SSH using a public key or SSH certificates if configured, and may login via the REST API with an API Token or OAuth JWTs if configured, and their authorization will be periodically refreshed from the LDAP server.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure the management directory service with your LDAP/AD server parameters, map your directory groups to Purity//FA roles, and rigorously test the connection before enabling it.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Directory Service panel, select the Array Management button, then click the edit icon.
• Enter your LDAP server URIs (using ldaps:// for encrypted connections), Base DN, Bind User, and Bind Password. Click Save.
• In the Roles section of the panel, click the edit icon. Map your Active Directory/LDAP groups to the corresponding Purity//FA RBAC roles (Array Admin, Storage Admin, Ops Admin, Read Only) by specifying the Group (Common Name) and Group Base (Organizational Unit). Click Save.
• Click Test to ensure the URIs resolve, the credentials bind successfully, and the mapped groups are found.
• Once the test passes, click the Configuration edit icon again, toggle Enabled to blue (true), and click Save.
From the CLI:
• Configure the directory service: Set the LDAP URIs, base DN, and bind credentials using the pureds setattr command.
• Command Syntax: pureds setattr --uri ldaps://<AD_SERVER>:636 -- base-dn <BASE_DN> --bind-user <BIND_USER> --bind-password management
• (Note: Purity will prompt interactively for the bind password to securely ingest it).
• Configure role-group mappings: Map your LDAP groups to array roles (e.g., array_admin).
• Command Syntax: pureds role setattr <ROLE> --group <AD_GROUP> -- group-base <OU>
• Example: pureds role setattr array_admin --group pureadmins -- group-base OU=Storage,DC=company,DC=com.
• Test the configuration: Run the directory service test to ensure connectivity and valid group configurations.
• Command Syntax: pureds test
• Enable the directory service: Only enable the service after the test successfully passes.
• Command Syntax: pureds enable management

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that a Directory Service is configured for array management, role-group mappings are defined to govern authorization, and that the configuration successfully passes diagnostic connectivity tests.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• Locate the Directory Service panel and select the Array Management view.
• Verify that the Enabled status is set to true.
• Review the configuration and verify that the URIs (preferably using ldaps://), Base DN, and Bind User are properly configured.
• Review the Roles section to confirm that role-group mappings (Array Admin, Storage Admin, Ops Admin, Read Only) are defined to control authorization.
• Test the configuration: Click Test in the upper-right corner of the panel to run the directory service diagnostic. Verify that resolving the URIs, binding and querying the tree, and finding the configured groups all return a PASSED status.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureds list management (or pureds list) to display the current directory service configuration. Verify the URI, Base DN, and Bind User fields are correct and the service is enabled.
• Run the command pureds role list to confirm that role-group mappings are securely defined for array roles.
• Test the configuration: Run the command pureds test to verify that the array can successfully resolve the URIs, bind to the directory using the credentials, and locate the mapped groups without errors.

Rule.title: Ensure only authorized local administrative accounts exist and a local emergency-access account is retained
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If your environment does not possess any mechanisms for delegated account management, or you have a need for additional local accounts for use as service accounts or for handling administration during network outages, FlashArray supports creating additional local administrative accounts.
If no management SAML configuration can be enabled, and no management LDAP directory service can be enabled, then Everpure recommends that you create one or more local administrators.

Rationale:
FlashArray can create local administrative accounts, and assign them a role to govern their permissions.
These accounts have a locally managed password and authorization policies. Local administrative users may also login via SSH using a public key or SSH certificates if configured, and may login via the REST API with an API Token or OAuth JWTs if configured.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, delete any local user accounts that are no longer authorized to access the FlashArray. Always ensure you maintain at least one local emergency access account with array_admin privileges in the event directory services or SAML become unavailable.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Users panel, click the Edit (three vertical dots) icon for the user account you want to remove and select Delete User....
• In the Delete User pop-up window, click Delete to confirm.
From the CLI:
• Delete an unauthorized or stale account using the pureadmin delete command.
• Command Syntax: pureadmin delete <USERNAME>
• Example: pureadmin delete obsolete_admin (Note: Once deleted, the user can no longer access the array, and deleted users cannot be restored).

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that all local administrative accounts on the array correspond to authorized users or active service accounts, and that any stale or former employee accounts have been removed.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• Under the Array tab, review the Users panel to inspect the list of configured local accounts.
• Compare this list against your organization's authorized personnel and service accounts, verifying that accounts for former employees or decommissioned services no longer exist.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureadmin list to enumerate all local administrator accounts.
• Review the output to confirm each account has a documented business justification and is actively required.

Rule.title: Ensure administrators and directory groups are granted least- privilege roles via management access policies
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray provides utilities for role based access controls, with 4 built-in management access policies, which can be assigned to administrators, directory service groups, or as the maximum role that can be granted by OAuth API Clients.
Management access policies may be dynamically created, allowing you to grant users different roles in different scopes (e.g. different realms). Everpure recommends the following:
• Use more than one management access policy if you possess multiple users administering the system.
• Create at least 1 realm in order to create logical units of management for the purpose of delegating administration.
• Grant users and groups only the permissions needed to perform their responsibilities, utilizing custom management access policies to limit user access to the scopes containing objects for which they are responsible.

Rationale:
FlashArray provides 4 built-in management access policies:
• array_admin: This policy has the "admin" role over the full array scope. This role can perform all administrative capabilities on the system, including management of other administrators, authentication mechanisms, IDPs, storage, and networking.
• storage_admin: This policy has the "storage" role over the full array scope. This role can manage all storage objects, such as file systems and snapshots, and can read all other system configurations such as networking.
• ops_admin: This policy has the "support" role over the full array scope. This role can manage supportability configurations, such as enabling remote assist, and can read all other system configurations.
• readonly: This policy has the "viewer" role over the full array scope. This role can read all system configurations.
The noted roles can be assigned to other scopes within management access policies in order to grant users with those policies those same permissions but in a different scope.
There are some limitations; physical networking and IDPs can only be managed by admins of the full array scope, though logical networking can still be managed by admins within a realm scope.
In order to reduce the risk of a compromised account, different administrators, or groups of administrators, should be assigned to the minimal role needed to accomplish their responsibilities. Granting every user full administrative privileges is a security risk.
This includes ensuring that realms are created as logical units to house configurations and data managed by a specific organization or team. Even if only one team within your organization currently utilizes FlashArray, creating a realm for that single team ensures that there will be no authorization risks or migrations if another team is granted use of the system with their own realm later.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, assign users and groups the minimum role needed to accomplish their responsibilities by leveraging Purity//FA's built-in or custom Management Access Policies.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• For Local Users: In the Users panel, click the edit (three vertical dots) icon for the user account and select Change Access Policy. Remove any overly permissive policies and assign the appropriate minimum-privilege policy.
• For Directory Service Groups: In the Directory Service panel, click the edit icon in the Roles section. Change the Active Directory/LDAP group mapping so that the group is mapped to the appropriate minimum-privilege RBAC role, then click Save.
From the CLI:
• Update a local user's access policy: Attach the correct minimum-privilege management access policy using pureadmin add, and remove the non-compliant policy using pureadmin remove.
• Command Syntax (Add): pureadmin add --access-policy <ACCESS_POLICY> <USERNAME>
• Command Syntax (Remove): pureadmin remove --access-policy <ACCESS_POLICY> <USERNAME>
• Example: pureadmin add --access-policy storage_admin admin1
• Update a directory service group mapping: Create or update the named mapping to attach an LDAP group to the correct Purity//FA access policy.
• Command Syntax: pureds role create <MAPPING_NAME> --access-policy <ACCESS_POLICY> --group <AD_GROUP> --group-base <OU>
• Example: pureds role create storagemap --access-policy storage_admin --group purestorageadmins --group-base OU=Storage,DC=company,DC=com

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that administrators and directory service groups are granted the minimum necessary privileges (e.g., readonly, storage_admin, ops_admin, or array_admin) using Management Access Policies.
Ensure that no user or group has an unnecessarily broad access policy assigned.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Users panel, review the Policies (or Access Policy) column for each local account to verify the appropriate privilege levels are assigned.
• In the Directory Service panel, review the Roles section to confirm that directory service group-to-role mappings are securely defined and align with the principle of least privilege.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureadmin list to display all local administrators.
• Review the Access Policy column in the output to confirm that each account has the appropriate minimum-privilege policy attached (and no account is unnecessarily set to array_admin).
• Run the command pureds role list to display the current LDAP/AD group to Purity//FA access policy mappings and verify their assignments.
• Run purepolicy management-access list to inspect the permissions, scopes, and aggregation strategies of all configured access policies.

Rule.title: Ensure SSH key-based authentication is configured for CLI access, preferably sourced from LDAP
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows for SSH public keys to be retrieved from a configurable attribute within a configured LDAP server if delegated account management with LDAP is in use.
If this is not viable in your environment, or local administrative accounts are in use, then SSH public key based authentication can be configured locally per-user.
Everpure recommends that SSH keys be retrieved from LDAP.

Rationale:
Retrieval of SSH keys from LDAP allows for authentication to be centrally managed, and ensures any compromised key can be removed from trust across your environment with a single change.
If this is not possible, individual administrators may configure SSH Public Keys for their accounts. This allows them to login with the corresponding private key instead of a password.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure SSH public keys for your administrative accounts so they can authenticate securely using a private key rather than a password.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Users panel, click the Edit (three vertical dots) icon for the user you want to modify and select Edit User....
• In the Edit User pop-up window, select Overwrite and paste the user's SSH public key into the Public Key field.
• Click Save.
From the CLI:
• Add a public key: Initiate the configuration for a specific user using the pureadmin setattr command.
• Command Syntax: pureadmin setattr --publickey <USERNAME>
• Action: Purity//FA will prompt you interactively to enter the public key. Paste the public key, press Enter to insert a new line, and then press CTRL-D to exit the prompt and save the key.
• Verify the key: Confirm the key was successfully registered.
• Command Syntax: pureadmin list --publickey <USERNAME>

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that SSH public keys are configured for users requiring CLI access (to prevent reliance on passwords) and test that the key- based authentication functions correctly.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Users panel, verify that a masked key is present in the Public Key column for each user who accesses the array via the CLI.
• Test the configuration: Using an SSH client (such as PuTTY or the native UNIX ssh command), attempt to log in to the FlashArray as the target user with the corresponding private key to verify that authentication succeeds without prompting for a password.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureadmin list --publickey to display all users and their public key status.
• Review the output to confirm that all authorized CLI users have a public key configured.
• Test the configuration: Initiate an SSH connection to the array from an administrative workstation using the user's private key to ensure successful authentication.

Rule.title: Ensure brute-force lockout is set to 3 attempts with a lockout duration of at least 1 hour
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports controls to prevent brute-force guessing of passwords. These controls cause a user to be locked out after a configurable number of consecutive failed password attempts. The lockout lasts for a configurable duration of time.
Everpure recommends the following:
• The number of consecutive password failures before lockout should be 3.
• The lockout duration should be no less than 1 hour.

Rationale:
Password login is necessary in many environments, but brute-force password guessing is always a risk that comes with it. Configuring brute-force protection can help mitigate that risk.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure the global password policy to enforce brute-force lockout protections and ensure the policy is actively enabled.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Password Policy.
• Modify the password policy settings: set the Maximum Login Attempts to 3 and the Lockout Duration to 60 (minutes).
• Ensure the policy is toggled to Enabled and click Save. (Note: If a legitimate administrator is inadvertently locked out, you must unlock their account manually from the CLI, as there is no specific GUI toggle documented for unlocking accounts in 6.9.x).
From the CLI:
• Configure the lockout thresholds: Set the lockout attributes on the global password policy (which applies to all local accounts) using the purepolicy password setattr command.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy password setattr --max-login-attempts <ATTEMPTS> --lockout-duration <DURATION> management
• Example: purepolicy password setattr --max-login-attempts 3 -- lockout-duration 60m management
• Enable the password policy: Ensure the management password policy is active.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy password enable management
• Unlock a locked account: If an administrator account is locked out and needs to be restored before the duration naturally expires, an array_admin can immediately reset the lockout.
• Command Syntax: pureadmin reset <USERNAME> --lockout
• Example: pureadmin reset admin1 --lockout

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the array is configured to lock out users after a maximum of 3 failed login attempts, with a lockout duration of at least 60 minutes.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Password Policy.
• Review the global password policy and verify the Maximum Login Attempts is set to 3 (or fewer, but greater than zero).
• Verify that the Lockout Duration is configured to at least 60 minutes.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purepolicy password list to display the configuration of the global password policy (named management).
• Review the output to confirm that the Enabled status is True.
• Review the Attribute and Value columns to confirm that Maximum Login Attempts is 3 or lower, and Lockout Duration is 60m or longer.
• (Optional) Run the command pureadmin list --lockout to display any users that are currently locked out by the system.

Rule.title: Ensure the password policy enforces 8+ characters, 3+ character groups, and username and dictionary checks
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports a password policy for administrative user passwords. It allows rules to be configured governing complexity requirements, such as minimum length, number of required unique character groups (e.g. letters, numbers, symbols), and whether a user's username may appear in their password.
Everpure recommends the following:
• The minimum password length should be 8 characters.
• The minimum number of character groups should be 3.
• The username check should be enabled.
• The dictionary check should be enabled.

Rationale:
Password login is necessary in many environments, so enforcing password complexity can help mitigate that risk of passwords being guessed.
Longer passwords with more complex character sets are harder to brute-force. Avoiding passwords containing an admin's username or common words can also help reduce the ability to brute force guess passwords.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure the global password policy to mandate longer passwords, require multiple character groups, and prevent the use of easily guessable dictionary words or usernames.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Password Policy.
• Set the Minimum Password Length to 8 (or more).
• Set the Minimum Character Groups to 3.
• Ensure the toggles for Enforce Username Check and Enforce Dictionary Check are enabled.
• Click Save.
From the CLI:
• Configure Length and Complexity: Set the minimum password length and character group requirements using the purepolicy password setattr command.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy password setattr --min-password-length <LENGTH> --min-character-groups <COUNT> management
• Example: purepolicy password setattr --min-password-length 8 -- min-character-groups 3 management
• Enable Dictionary and Username Checks: Enable the specific security checks on the management password policy using the purepolicy password enable command.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy password enable --username-check -- dictionary-check management

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the array enforces strong password complexity for local administrators, specifically requiring a minimum length of 8 characters, at least 3 character groups, and actively enforcing both dictionary and username checks.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Password Policy.
• Verify the Minimum Password Length is set to at least 8 characters.
• Verify the Minimum Character Groups requirement is set to at least 3.
• Verify that the Enforce Username Check and Enforce Dictionary Check toggles are enabled.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purepolicy password list to display the current configuration of the global password policy (named management).
• Review the output to confirm the following Attribute and Value pairs are compliant:
• Minimum Password Length is 8 or greater.
• Minimum Character Groups is 3 or greater.
• Enforce Dictionary Check is True.
• Enforce Username Check is True.

Rule.title: Ensure OAuth API clients use least-privilege access policies and access-token TTLs of 60 minutes or less
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports configuring one or more identity providers for API Clients. These IDPs can then issue identity tokens to any user on the array that can be exchanged with the array for API access using the OAuth2 standard.
The configuration also allows you to specify maximum permissions that can be granted to users who receive id tokens from the IDP, as well as the TTL for access tokens issued to clients.
Everpure recommends the following:
• All API Clients should be configured with appropriately limited permissions based on the use case of the IDP.
• All API Clients should be configured with a TTL of 60 minutes or fewer.

Rationale:
The OAuth2 specification allows for short-lived access tokens to be issued and used for API access. Use of short-lived tokens can substantially reduce the impact of a compromise, as the tokens have a limited window of use.
Limiting the granted permissions for API Clients can also have value. If a user desires to run API automation, such as workload performance monitoring, or snapshot management, it is not necessary to authorize that automation with the full permissions of the user.
By utilizing an appropriately configured OAuth API Client, you can restrict applications to readonly or storage_admin permissions, even when they act on behalf of a user who may be an array_admin. This limits the impact of a compromised application on the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, delete or disable inactive API clients, and ensure all active clients are bound to restrictive access policies with short-lived tokens.
(Note: Modifying or deleting an active API client will immediately invalidate its issued tokens, so changes should be coordinated with the teams responsible for those integrations).
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the API Clients panel, select any unused clients and click the trash icon to delete them.
• For active clients, click the edit icon to reduce the assigned access policy or shorten the token TTL as appropriate.
• To create a new compliant client, click the + (Create API Client) icon. In the pop- up window, enter the client name, select a minimum access policy (e.g., readonly), set the time to live (e.g., 1h), and paste the RSA public key in PEM format, then click Create.
From the CLI:
• Disable an unused API client: Use the pureapiclient disable command to temporarily revoke a client's access.
• Command Syntax: pureapiclient disable <CLIENT_NAME>
• Delete an unused API client: Use the pureapiclient delete command to permanently remove an obsolete client.
• Command Syntax: pureapiclient delete <CLIENT_NAME>
• Create a new, least-privilege API client: Use the pureapiclient create command, specifying a restrictive access policy and a short token TTL.
• Command Syntax: pureapiclient create --access-policy readonly -- access-token-ttl 1h --public-key <CLIENT_NAME>
• Action: Purity//FA will prompt you interactively to enter the public key. Paste the public key, press Enter to insert a new line, and then press CTRL-D to exit the prompt and create the client.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that all configured API clients have a documented business purpose, are assigned the minimum necessary permissions (e.g., readonly instead of array_admin), and utilize short-lived access tokens (TTL of 60 minutes or less) to reduce the impact of a compromised token.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• Scroll to the API Clients panel and review the list of configured API clients.
• Verify each active API client has a documented business purpose.
• Review the access policy and TTL assigned to each client to ensure they enforce the principle of least privilege.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureapiclient list to display all configured API clients.
• Review the output to verify the Access Policy, Enabled status, and token TTL for each client.
• Verify no API clients are enabled that are no longer actively in use.

Rule.title: Ensure static REST API tokens are used only when necessary and configured to expire periodically
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports administrators creating static API for REST API access. This should only be utilized in cases where OAuth usage is not feasible.
Everpure recommends the following:
• REST API tokens can be configured to expire. If REST API tokens are configured, configure them to expire periodically.
• Only create REST API tokens if no API Clients for OAuth can be created and enabled for REST access.
• If REST API tokens are configured, it is highly recommended that you monitor which IP addresses access the REST API.

Rationale:
API Tokens are a custom mechanism for REST API access, with no standardized mechanism for rotation. As such, changing them is more difficult. But making them non- expiring increases the risk of compromise, because a one-time exposure of the token can lead to compromise for an indefinite window of time.
API Tokens also act exactly as the user who creates them, with full permissions. So an API token created by an array_admin for something like performance monitoring can still act with full array_admin rights. As such, a compromised application using API Tokens cannot have the impact limited by compensating controls around the role assigned to the token.
As such, the only compensating control to reduce the impact of a compromised API Token are network access controls to the REST API.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, delete unauthorized or stale API tokens, and ensure that any newly issued tokens are configured with a strict validity period (timeout) so they expire automatically.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Users panel, click the Edit icon for the user you want to modify.
• To delete a token: Select Remove API Token... and click Remove to confirm.
• To rotate or create an expiring token: Select Create API Token... (or Recreate API Token... to overwrite an existing one). In the prompt, enter a validity period in the Expires In field so the token does not live indefinitely, then click Create.
From the CLI:
• Delete an existing API token:
• Command Syntax: pureadmin delete --api-token <USERNAME>
• Create a new API token with an expiration: Ensure you use the --timeout flag to enforce an expiry period (e.g., s, m, h, d, or w).
• Command Syntax: pureadmin create --api-token --timeout <PERIOD> <USERNAME>
• Example: pureadmin create --api-token --timeout 30d pureuser
• Retrieve the new token for the consumer:
• Command Syntax: pureadmin list --api-token --expose <USERNAME> (Note: Store the token securely in a secrets manager. Never embed tokens in plaintext configuration files).

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that static API tokens are only issued when OAuth usage is not feasible, that tokens are assigned only to accounts with the minimum necessary privileges, and that tokens are configured to expire periodically to reduce the risk of long-term compromise.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Users panel under the Array tab, check the API Token column to see which users have a masked token present.
• For users with a token, click the Edit (three vertical dots) icon and select Show API Token... to view the token details.
• Review the token creation and expiry dates. Verify that only accounts actively requiring API access have tokens, and that they enforce an appropriate expiration timeframe.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureadmin list --api-token to list all accounts and their API token status.
• Review the Created and Expires columns to identify tokens that lack an expiration date (indicated by a -) or have existed longer than the organization's rotation policy allows.
• Verify that each token-holding account is assigned the minimum required management access policy.

Rule.title: Ensure administrative audit logs are forwarded to remote syslog or monitored via the REST API
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray creates administrative audit records for all administrative operations that cause a change to the system configuration or state.
Everpure recommends that these logs be monitored via REST API, or sent to configured remote syslog servers in order to detect suspicious or unexpected activity and respond accordingly.

Rationale:
The FlashArray administrative audit records track the following information for every operation that changes configuration or state:
• The time when it was performed
• The user who performed the action
• The origin array they performed the action from (in case it was performed from another array in the fleet)
• The equivalent CLI command, sub-command, and arguments representing the change that was performed These pieces of information are valuable for detecting changes to the system state in unexpected configuration areas, by unexpected users, or originating from unexpected locations.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, implement continuous monitoring by configuring external syslog forwarding or REST API integration, and establish a process to review unexpected configurations.
From the GUI:
• To Configure Syslog Forwarding:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the Syslog Servers panel, click the + (Create) icon.
• Enter the URI of your remote syslog server (e.g., tcp://10.10.10.10:514) and click Create.
• To Configure REST API Monitoring:
• Integrate your SIEM or monitoring tool using the Pure Storage REST API endpoints to continuously poll for audit trail events.
• Establish a Review Process: Ensure your monitoring team or SIEM alerts analyze the logs specifically for unexpected Users, Origin arrays, or Commands that change system state.
From the CLI:
• To Configure Syslog Forwarding: Create a remote syslog server destination using the purelog syslog create command.
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog create --uri <URI> <SERVER_NAME>
• Establish a Review Process: If manually reviewing, use the pureaudit list command periodically. You can isolate specific users or times using the --filter flag (e.g., pureaudit list --filter "user='pureuser'").

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that audit logs are continuously monitored — either by forwarding them to a remote syslog server or by polling them via the REST API — and that reviewers are checking the time, user, origin array, and executed commands.
From the GUI:
• Verify Syslog Forwarding: Navigate to Settings > System. In the Syslog Servers panel, verify that at least one remote syslog server is actively configured to receive audit events.
• Verify Manual/API Log Access: Navigate to Settings > Access and scroll to the Audit Trail pane. Confirm logs are accessible and capture the Time, User, Origin, and Command fields.
• Verify REST API (If Syslog is not used): Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies (API Clients pane) and verify that an active API Client or service account exists for your SIEM/monitoring platform to poll the REST API.
From the CLI:
• Verify Syslog Forwarding: Run the command purelog syslog list. Review the output to confirm a remote syslog server URI is configured.
• Verify Audit Records: Run the command pureaudit list (or pureaudit list -- filter "time >= '<YYYY-MM-DD>'" for recent events). Review the output to ensure the Time, User, Command, and Arguments are being accurately recorded.
• Verify REST API (If Syslog is not used): Verify with your monitoring teams that an active external script or tool is successfully authenticating and pulling the audit logs via the FlashArray REST API.

Rule.title: Ensure administrative session logs are forwarded to remote syslog or monitored via the REST API
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray creates administrative session records for all administrative logins and logouts, whether successful or unsuccessful.
Everpure recommends that these logs be monitored via REST API, or sent to configured remote syslog servers in order to detect suspicious or unexpected activity and respond accordingly.
Everpure recommends that you monitor these logs in order to detect use of weak authentication mechanisms.

Rationale:
The FlashArray administrative session logs track the following information for every attempted or successful login, and logout:
• The time when it occurred or began
• The time when the session ended, if login had been successful
• The user associated with the login
• The product interface where the login was attempted (e.g. CLI)
• The IP address they performed the login from
• The event itself (e.g. failed authentication, "login" if the user has not yet logged out, or "user session" for a completed session)
• The method used to attempt authentication (e.g. certificate, saml2_sso, password, public key)
• The event count, which is greater than 1 if multiple failed login attempts occurred in a short period of time These pieces of information are valuable for detecting attempted or successful intrusion into the system, use of compromised keys for login, or logins originating from unexpected locations.
These pieces of information can also be used to detect logins made using unexpected credentials (e.g. a user logging in with an API Token when OAuth is available; a user logging in with a password when SSH public keys are configured).</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, implement continuous monitoring by configuring external syslog forwarding or REST API integration for session logs, and establish a process to review logs for weak authentication methods or unexpected access.
From the GUI:
• Establish a Review Process: Create a standard operating procedure to regularly review the Session Log pane under Settings > Access specifically looking for unexpected IP locations or failed authentication events.
• To Configure Syslog Forwarding: Navigate to Settings > System. In the Syslog Servers panel, click the + (Create) icon, enter your remote syslog server URI, and click Create.
• To Configure REST API Monitoring: Integrate your SIEM or monitoring tool using the Pure Storage REST API endpoints to continuously poll for session events.
Note: If credentials are believed to be compromised, immediately rotate the affected account's password using the Users pane and rotate API tokens.
From the CLI:
• Establish a Review Process: Implement an operational procedure to periodically run puresession list and review the output for unexpected session activity.
• To Configure Syslog Forwarding: Create a remote syslog server destination using the purelog syslog create command.
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog create --uri <URI> <SERVER_NAME>
• Example: purelog syslog create --uri tcp://10.10.10.10:514 syslog- server01

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that administrative session logs are continuously monitored — either by forwarding them to a remote syslog server or by polling them via the REST API — and that reviewers are checking the start/end times, users, access interfaces, IP locations, and event types.
From the GUI:
• Verify Manual/API Log Access: Navigate to Settings > Access and locate the Session Log pane. Confirm logs are accessible and capture the Start Time, End Time, Interface, User, Location, and Event fields.
• Verify Syslog Forwarding: Navigate to Settings > System. In the Syslog Servers panel, verify that a remote syslog server is actively configured to receive events.
• Verify REST API (If Syslog is not used): Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies (API Clients pane) to verify an active API Client exists for your SIEM/monitoring platform to poll session logs via the REST API.
From the CLI:
• Verify Session Records: Run the command puresession list to display user session logs. Review the output to ensure Start Time, End Time, Interface, User, Location, and Event fields are being actively recorded.
• Verify Syslog Forwarding: Run the command purelog syslog list to confirm a remote syslog server URI is configured.
• Verify REST API (If Syslog is not used): Verify with your monitoring teams that an external script is successfully polling the FlashArray REST API for session records.

Rule.title: Ensure system alerts are actively monitored via remote syslog or email alert watchers
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray creates alerts for a variety of system conditions that may be cause for concern. Not all of these are security related, but a number of them are either directly security related or can have an impact on security.
Everpure recommends that these alerts be monitored via REST API, or sent via syslog to configured remote syslog servers, via email using the configured SMTP relay, or via remote SNMP managers, in order to detect alerts of concern and respond accordingly.

Rationale:
The FlashArray alerts cover a variety of cases, including but not limited to:
• Expiring certificates
• Insecure default credentials in use
• Drive removal
• Hardware cable removal
• Snapshot limits being approached Some alerts, such as default credentials, directly impact security. However, even for alerts that do not always directly pertain to security, they can potentially indicate attempts at physical tampering with the system, such as blade removal, or indicate system states that impact other security controls, such as approaching snapshot limits that impact data protection.
As such, alerts should be appropriately monitored and acted upon.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, implement a continuous alerting process by configuring an email alert watcher or remote syslog forwarding (or both).
From the GUI:
• To Configure Alert Watchers (Email):
• Navigate to Settings > System and select Alerts and Notifications in the navigation pane.
• Add the appropriate internal email address for your organization's monitoring or administrative team to receive alert notifications.
• To Configure Syslog Forwarding:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the Syslog Servers panel, create a syslog server by entering the URI of your remote syslog server (e.g., tcp://10.10.10.10:514) and saving the configuration.
From the CLI:
• To Configure Alert Watchers (Email): Add a designated email address using the purealert watcher create command.
• Command Syntax: purealert watcher create <EMAIL_ADDRESS>
• Example: purealert watcher create soc-alerts@mycompany.com
• To Configure Syslog Forwarding: Create a remote syslog server destination using the purelog syslog create command.
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog create --uri <URI> <SERVER_NAME>
• Example: purelog syslog create --uri tcp://10.10.10.10:514 syslog- server01

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that array alerts are actively monitored — either by forwarding them to a remote syslog server or by configuring an internal email address (alert watcher) — to ensure timely notification of security and system events.
From the GUI:
• Verify Alert Watchers (Email): Navigate to Settings > System and select Alerts and Notifications from the left navigation pane. Verify that at least one valid internal email address is listed to receive alerts.
• Verify Syslog Forwarding: Navigate to Settings > System. Locate the Syslog Servers panel and verify that a remote syslog server is actively configured to receive alert messages.
From the CLI:
• Verify Alert Watchers (Email): Run the command purealert watcher list.
Review the output to ensure that an internal organization email address is configured and enabled to receive notifications.
• Verify Syslog Forwarding: Run the command purelog syslog list. Review the output to confirm that a remote syslog server URI is actively configured to receive events (which includes purity.alert records).

Rule.title: Ensure at least one alert watcher is configured to receive alerts of all severities
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows configuration of one or more alert watchers, which are email addresses that will receive emails for new system alerts. The minimum severity of alerts that will be sent to each watcher is also configurable.
Everpure recommends that you configure at least 1 alert watcher that receives alerts of all severities.

Rationale:
While it may be helpful to have some administrators or monitors only receive emails about critical system alerts, responding to or monitoring alerts of lower severity can help ensure that they do not become critical.
As such Everpure recommends that you have at least 1 alert watcher that receives all alerts.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure an organizational email address to monitor array alerts.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System and select Alerts and Notifications.
• In the Alert Watchers panel, click the + (Create) icon, enter the desired email address, and click Create.
• To adjust the notification level, click the More Options menu next to the newly created watcher, select Edit, choose the minimum severity, and click Save.
• Ensure the Enabled switch is toggled on.
From the CLI:
• Create the watcher: Run the purealert watcher create command.
• Command Syntax: purealert watcher create <EMAIL_ADDRESS>
• Set the severity level: Configure the minimum notification severity through an alert-watcher policy rule.
o Command Syntax: purepolicy alert-watcher rule add --email <EMAIL_ADDRESS> --minimum-notification-severity {critical|info|warning} <ALERT_POLICY>
o Alternatively, update an existing rule: purepolicy alert-watcher rule setattr --rule-name <RULE> --minimum-notification-severity {critical|info|warning} <ALERT_POLICY>
o Example: purepolicy alert-watcher rule add --email soc- alerts@mycompany.com --minimum-notification-severity info alert_policy_main
• Enable the watcher: Ensure the watcher is actively receiving alerts using the purealert watcher enable command.
• Command Syntax: purealert watcher enable <EMAIL_ADDRESS>

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least one organizational email address is configured as an alert watcher to receive all system alerts.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System and select Alerts and Notifications in the left navigation pane.
• Locate the Alert Watchers panel.
• Verify that at least one active, organizational email address is configured (in addition to the built-in purestorage.com address).
• Verify that the Enabled toggle is active (blue).
From the CLI:
• Run the command purealert watcher list to display configured alert recipients.
• Review the output to confirm an organizational email address is present and its status is enabled.
• Verify that the Minimum Notification Severity is set to info so that the watcher receives alerts of all severities. (Note: The CLI command output will show the active severity levels)

Rule.title: Ensure at least one remote management syslog server is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows the creation of management syslog servers. These servers receive messages for administrative audit logs, administrative session logs, and alerts.
Everpure recommends that you configure at least 1 management syslog server.

Rationale:
Syslog servers allow proactive push notifications of changes and events on the system, which can allow for real-time detection and response to unexpected events.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure at least one management syslog server to allow for real-time detection and response to unexpected events.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the Syslog Servers panel, click the + (Create) icon.
• Enter the URI of your remote syslog server (e.g., tls://10.10.10.10:6514) and provide a name.
• Click Create to apply the configuration.
From the CLI:
• Configure a remote syslog server destination using the purelog syslog create command.
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog create --uri <URI> <NAME>
• Example: purelog syslog create --uri tls://10.10.10.10:6514 syslog-server01

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least one remote management syslog server is configured to receive proactive push notifications for administrative audit logs, session logs, and alerts.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• Locate the Syslog Servers panel.
• Verify that at least one remote syslog server is actively configured to receive events.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purelog syslog list.
• Review the output to confirm that at least one remote syslog server URI is actively configured.

Rule.title: Ensure array TLS certificates are CA-signed, adequately sized, and rotated at least every 90 days
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows certificates on the system to be centrally managed. This includes both "array-type" certificates, which the FlashArray storage array can use to represent itself to clients, and "external-type" certificates which can be the public certificates of certificate authorities that sign the certificates of other environmental resources or the public certificates of self-signed environmental resources.
Everpure recommends the following:
• All RSA certificates in use should have at least 2048-bit keys.
• All ECDSA certificates in use should have at least 256-bit keys.
• Only "external-type" certificates should be used as roots of trust for other environmental resources.
• All "array-type" certificates should be signed by a certificate authority.
• All "array-type" certificates should have a lifetime of at most 90 days.

Rationale:
RSA and ECDSA Key size recommendations are in-line with NIST standards to ensure cryptographic strength.
Using "external-type" certificates as roots of trust ensures that it is not possible to mistakenly upload a private key to the system for a configuration that does not require it.
Ensuring all "array-type" certificates are signed by a trusted certificate authority ensures that clients, whether for administrative TLS, S3, or another protocol can use a strong root of trust for communication with FlashArray. It also allows rotation of certificates to be done with no client disruption.
Rotating certificates periodically reduces the impact of a compromised private key.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, generate a properly sized Certificate Signing Request (CSR), have it signed by your CA for a maximum of 90 days, import it, and manage your roots of trust using external certificates.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System and locate the SSL Certificate / Array Certificates panel.
• Click the menu icon and select Construct Certificate Signing Request. Fill in the required attributes and ensure the key size meets the 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit ECDSA minimums. Click Create and download the CSR.
• Submit the CSR to your organization's trusted Certificate Authority and request that the signed certificate has a lifetime of 90 days or less.
• Once the CA returns the signed certificate, return to the GUI, click the menu icon, and select Import Certificate to replace the existing certificate.
• To configure roots of trust, navigate to the External Certificates panel and import the trusted CA's public certificates.
• Establish an operational process to rotate the array-type certificates every 90 days.
From the CLI:
• Prepare the Key & CSR: Construct a Certificate Signing Request using the purecert csr create command. (Note: Purity uses RSA 2048 by default. If you need to change the key algorithm to ECDSA or increase the key size, first run purecert self-signed setattr --new-key --key-algorithm <ALGORITHM> --key-size <SIZE> before generating the CSR.)
• Command Syntax: purecert csr create <NAME> --common-name <FQDN>
• Submit the generated CSR block to your Certificate Authority and request a signed certificate with a validity period of 90 days or less.
• Import the Signed Certificate: Once the CA returns the signed certificate, import it using the purecert imported setattr command. (Append the -- intermediate-certificate flag if required).
• Command Syntax: purecert imported setattr <NAME>
• Import Roots of Trust: Ensure any CA root certificates are imported as external certificates rather than array certificates.
• Establish a continuous operational process (such as a scheduled automation script) to rotate these certificates every 90 days.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the array uses an appropriately sized, CA-signed certificate with a maximum lifetime of 90 days, and that external certificates are properly utilized for roots of trust.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System and locate the SSL Certificate panel.
• In the Array Certificates panel, click the active management certificate to view its details.
• Verify the following attributes for the array certificate:
• Key Size is at least 2048 (for RSA) or 256 (for ECDSA).
• Issuer is a trusted internal or public Certificate Authority (not "Everpure" or "Self- Signed").
• The duration between the Valid From and Valid To dates is 90 days or less.
• Scroll to the External Certificates panel and verify that any certificates used as roots of trust are configured here (ensuring they are external-type).
From the CLI:
• Run the command purecert list to display the active certificates on the array.
• Review the output to ensure the following for your array type certificates:
• The Issuer is a trusted Certificate Authority.
• The Key Size is at least 2048 (for RSA) or 256 (for ECDSA).
• The difference between the Valid From and Valid To dates does not exceed 90 days.
• Verify that roots of trust are explicitly stored and listed under the external Type.

Rule.title: Ensure SAML SSO uses HTTPS with encrypted assertions and signed requests
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>SAML may be used for delegated authentication across various protocols on FlashArray. The array URL, IDP metadata URL, and IDP URL are all required to use https if specified.
IDP Metadata URL usage is optional; if one is not used, then you may instead manually configure the IDP URL, verification certificate, and IDP entity ID.
It is recommended that encrypted assertions from the IDP be enabled if your IDP supports them, and a decryption certificate be configured.
It is recommended that signed requests from the array be enabled if your IDP supports them, and a signing credential be configured.

Rationale:
Encrypted assertions prevent the SAML assertions from your IDP from being read by entities other than the FlashArray array. This ensures that any sensitive information that may be in such assertions, such as PII, roles, or group memberships cannot be read by unintended actors.
Signed requests from the array ensure that the array cannot be impersonated in requests to the IDP. This prevents malicious actors from forging requests to your IDP in order to attempt to obtain information about arbitrary users or services.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your SAML2 SSO configuration to require HTTPS, signed requests, and encrypted assertions using dedicated credentials.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies and scroll to the SAML2 SSO pane.
• Click the edit icon for the Configuration.
• Update the Array URL and IdP URL fields to ensure they begin with https://.
• Enable Signed Requests: Slide the Sign Request toggle to the right (blue) and enter your array's signing certificate name in the Signing Credential field.
• Enable Encrypted Assertions: Slide the Encrypt Assertion toggle to the right (blue) and enter your array's decryption certificate name in the Decryption Credential field.
• If the Verification Certificate is expired or self-signed, click Edit to paste the new PEM-formatted certificate from your IdP.
• Click Save. (Note: Always perform an E2E Test from the GUI after making SAML changes to ensure administrative access is not interrupted).
From the CLI:
• Secure the SAML configuration: Update the URLs to HTTPS and set the signing/decryption credentials with puresso saml2 setattr, then turn on request signing and assertion encryption with puresso saml2 enable.
• Command Syntax (set URLs and credentials): puresso saml2 setattr -- array-url https://<ARRAY_FQDN> --idp-url https://<IDP_URL> -- signing-credential <CRED_NAME> --decryption-credential <CRED_NAME> <IDP_NAME>
• Command Syntax (enable signing and encryption): puresso saml2 enable -- sign-request --encrypt-assertion <IDP_NAME>
• Update the Verification Certificate: If the IdP certificate is expired or self- signed, replace it using the --verification-certificate flag.
• Command Syntax: puresso saml2 setattr --verification-certificate <IDP_NAME>
• Action: Paste the new PEM-formatted certificate at the interactive prompt, press Enter, and then press Ctrl-D.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the SAML SSO integration strictly utilizes HTTPS for all communication URLs, enforces encrypted assertions from the Identity Provider (IdP) to prevent interception, and enforces signed requests from the FlashArray to prevent impersonation.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies and scroll to the SAML2 SSO pane.
• Review the configured URLs ( Array URL, IdP URL, or Metadata URL) to verify they all utilize the https:// scheme.
• Click the edit icon for the Configuration.
• Verify that the Sign Request toggle is enabled (blue) and that a valid Signing Credential is configured.
• Verify that the Encrypt Assertion toggle is enabled (blue) and that a valid Decryption Credential is configured.
• Verify that the Verification Certificate is present, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority, and has not expired.
From the CLI:
• Display the full SAML2 SSO configuration and certificate details by running the command puresso saml2 list --verification-certificate.
• Review the output to confirm that the Array URL and IdP URL fields begin with https://.
• Verify that the Sign Request and Encrypt Assertion attributes are set to True.
• Review the Verification Certificate details to ensure it was issued by a trusted CA and the Valid To date is not expired.

Rule.title: Ensure Active Directory accounts are configured to require TLS
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports native integration with Active Directory domains in order to enable LDAP lookups for authorization, and Kerberos authentication.
FlashArray does this by creating a computer account in the domain to represent itself and generate kerberos keys. A unique AD account may be created for each server on the array that needs one.
Everpure recommends that you configure TLS as required for all AD accounts. This is the default.

Rationale:
While Active Directory supports non-TLS LDAP communication, it is less secure than TLS and allows for traffic to potentially be tampered with or exposed.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your Active Directory account configuration to explicitly require TLS for all domain controller communications.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies or Storage > Servers depending on where the AD account is applied.
• Edit the Active Directory configuration (e.g., in the Configure Remote Directory Service window).
• Under the TLS Mode setting, select the required radio button to force TLS communication with the domain controller.
• Click Create (or Save) to apply the configuration.
From the CLI:
• Update the Active Directory account to require TLS using the puread account setattr command.
• Command Syntax: puread account setattr --tls required <NAME>
• Example: puread account setattr --tls required server1::ad-ad

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the array's Active Directory (AD) integration accounts are configured to require TLS, ensuring secure communication and preventing potential traffic tampering or exposure.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies (for array management AD accounts) or navigate to Storage > Servers and select your file server (for file service AD accounts).
• Locate the Active Directory Accounts or Remote Directory Service panel.
• Open the configuration details for the connected AD account.
• Verify that the TLS Mode is set to required.
From the CLI:
• Run the command puread account list to display information about Active Directory account attributes.
• Review the output and verify that the TLS column for the configured AD account is set to required (rather than optional).

Rule.title: Ensure LDAP directory services use LDAPS with a configured CA root of trust
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports LDAP directory services for administrative login and authorization, as well as for NFS authorization.
Everpure recommends the following:
• Utilize LDAPS in order to establish secure LDAP connections.
• Specify one or more certificate authorities as roots of trust for each LDAP directory service.

Rationale:
Encrypting LDAP communication with TLS is crucial to prevent malicious actors from inspecting or tampering with LDAP traffic pertaining to authorization.
Proper roots of trust are important for ensuring the TLS authenticity cannot be compromised, and such TLS traffic cannot be intercepted.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your directory service configuration to enforce LDAPS and configure the appropriate CA certificate for trust.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Directory Service panel, select either the Array Management or Data button, then click the edit icon.
• Update the URIs field to use the ldaps:// scheme (e.g., ldaps://ldap.company.com:636) and click Save.
• To configure the root of trust, click Edit next to CA Certificate within the Directory Service panel. Paste the PEM-formatted certificate from your Certificate Authority and click Save. (Note: The CA certificate is only used/applicable for the Array Management service, not the Data service).
From the CLI:
• Update the URI to LDAPS: Modify the directory service URI using the pureds setattr command.
• Command Syntax: pureds setattr --uri ldaps://<LDAP_SERVER>:<PORT> <SERVICE-NAME>
• Example: pureds setattr --uri ldaps://dc01.domain.com:636 management
• Verify the Configuration:
• Run pureds list to ensure the URI successfully updated.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the LDAP directory services utilize LDAPS to establish secure connections and that a Certificate Authority (CA) is configured as a root of trust.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• Locate the Directory Service panel.
• Select either the Array Management or Data view.
• Verify that the URIs field begins with ldaps:// rather than ldap://.
• Verify that a CA Certificate is configured by checking the CA Certificate field in the panel.
From the CLI:
• Inspect the directory service configuration by running the command pureds list.
• Review the output and confirm the URI field uses the ldaps:// scheme.
• Verify that a CA certificate is configured by running the command pureds list --ca- certificate.

Rule.title: Ensure syslog servers use TLS with a configured CA root of trust
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports configuring remote syslog servers to receive a variety of different messages, including administrative and data audit records, session records, and alerts.
Everpure recommends the following:
• Configure all syslog servers to use TLS to protect traffic from inspection and tampering.
• Configure one or more certificate authorities as roots of trust for syslog servers.

Rationale:
Syslog messages for audits, sessions, etc. are important for detection and response pipelines. As such it is prudent to ensure they cannot be tampered with.
Some such information can also be considered sensitive or contain PII, and so avoiding disclosure of their contents is also important.
As such, proper roots of trust are important for ensuring the TLS authenticity cannot be compromised, and such TLS traffic cannot be intercepted.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure your syslog servers to use TLS encryption and import a CA certificate to authenticate the remote servers.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the Syslog Servers panel, remove any existing plaintext syslog entries.
• Enter the URI of your remote syslog server using the tls:// scheme (e.g., tls://10.10.10.10:6514).
• Click the Add button to add the URI to the list of syslog server output locations.
From the CLI:
• Delete the existing plaintext syslog server:
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog delete <SERVER_NAME>
• Add a TLS-encrypted syslog server:
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog create --uri tls://<SYSLOG_HOST>:<PORT> <NAME>
• Import the CA certificate for syslog: Purity//FA's syslog agent uses this certificate to authenticate itself to the remote syslog servers.
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog global setattr --ca-certificate
• Action: Paste the PEM-formatted certificate at the interactive prompt.
• Verify the new configuration:
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog list

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that configured syslog servers use TLS and that a Certificate Authority (CA) certificate is configured as a root of trust for syslog communications.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• Locate the Syslog Servers panel.
• Verify that the URI for each configured server uses the tls:// scheme.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purelog syslog list. Review the output to confirm the URI field uses the tls:// scheme rather than udp:// or tcp://.
• Run the command purelog syslog global list --ca-certificate to verify that a CA certificate is imported for authenticating syslog servers.

Rule.title: Ensure the SMTP relay host is configured with STARTTLS encryption and authentication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports configuring a relayhost for the simple mail transfer protocol (SMTP) for the purpose of ensuring email delivery for alert emails.
Everpure recommends the following:
• Configure an SMTP relayhost.
• Configure the starttls encryption mode for SMTP.
• Configure authentication for your SMTP relayhost, if it supports it.

Rationale:
SMTP relayhosts improve the reliability of email delivery, helping to avoid issues that can cause missed alerts. Enforcing TLS between FlashArray and the relayhost prevents tampering and disclosure of email contents.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your SMTP configuration to specify your relay host, enforce TLS encryption, and configure authentication credentials.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System and locate the Alert Routing (Relay Host) panel.
• Enter your SMTP Relay Host address.
• Set the Encryption Mode to starttls.
• If authentication is required, enter the Username and Password.
• Click Save.
From the CLI:
• Configure the relay host and enforce TLS: Use the puresmtp setattr command to specify your server and set the encryption mode to starttls.
• Command Syntax: puresmtp setattr --relay-host <HOST> --encryption- mode starttls
• Example: puresmtp setattr --relay-host smtp.mycompany.com -- encryption-mode starttls
• Configure Authentication (if required): If your SMTP server requires authentication, append the --username and --password flags.
• Command Syntax: puresmtp setattr --username <USERNAME> --password
• Action: Purity will prompt you interactively to enter and retype the password.

check.check-content:
