To align with the security recommendations, verify that an SMTP relay host is configured, it enforces TLS encryption (starttls), and authentication is utilized if supported by your relay host.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System and locate the Alert Routing (Relay Host) panel.
• Verify that a Relay Host is configured.
• Verify that the Encryption Mode is set to starttls.
• If your relay requires authentication, verify that a Username is configured.
From the CLI:
• Display the current SMTP configuration by running the command puresmtp list.
• Review the output to verify the following:
• A valid Relay Host is configured.
• The Encryption Mode is set to starttls.
• If your SMTP server requires it, the Username field is populated (indicating authentication is configured).

Rule.title: Ensure SNMP, if enabled, uses SNMPv3 with SHA authentication and AES privacy
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports configuring the simple network management protocol (SNMP). An SNMP agent can be configured on the array, allowing external clients to query the array using SNMP for information such as performance metrics and array details.
SNMP managers can also be configured to receive alerts.
Everpure recommends that you do not utilize SNMP unless your environment requires it.
If SNMP is enabled, Everpure recommends the following:
• Utilize SNMPv3, not SNMPv2c.
• Configure an authentication passphrase with SHA as the authentication protocol.
The authentication passphrase should be 8 characters or longer, and sufficiently complex.
• Configure a privacy passphrase with AES as the privacy protocol. The privacy passphrase should be 8 characters or longer, and sufficiently complex.

Rationale:
SNMP as a protocol is necessary in some environments, where retrieving metrics and configuration via a REST API may not be feasible, or where email or syslog delivery of alerts may not be available.
SNMPv2c has weak authentication, and should not be used.
When using SNMPv3, it is important to use strong passwords for authentication and privacy.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your SNMP configuration to utilize SNMPv3 with strong authentication and privacy protocols, and ensure passphrases meet the 8-character minimum complexity requirement.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the SNMP panel, click the menu icon and select Add SNMP Manager (or click Edit for an existing manager).
• Complete the following fields in the dialog box:
• SNMP Version: Select v3.
• User: Enter the recognized User ID.
• Auth Protocol: Select SHA.
• Auth Passphrase: Enter a complex passphrase of at least 8 characters.
• Privacy Protocol: Select AES.
• Privacy Passphrase: Enter a complex passphrase of at least 8 characters.
• Click Create (or Save). (Note: To secure the built-in localhost agent, click the Edit (pencil) icon next to it and apply the same v3, SHA, and AES settings).
From the CLI:
• Configure an SNMP Manager: Create or update an SNMP manager to enforce v3, SHA, and AES using the puresnmp create or puresnmp setattr command.
• Command Syntax: puresnmp create --host <HOST> --version v3 --user <USER> --auth-protocol SHA --auth-passphrase --privacy-protocol AES --privacy-passphrase <MANAGER_NAME>
• Action: Purity will prompt you interactively to enter and retype the authentication and privacy passphrases. Ensure both are at least 8 characters long.
• Secure the local agent: Update the built-in localhost agent to require SNMPv3.
• Command Syntax: puresnmp setattr --version v3 --user <USER> -- auth-protocol SHA --auth-passphrase --privacy-protocol AES -- privacy-passphrase localhost

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that if SNMP is utilized, it is strictly configured for SNMPv3 with an authentication protocol of SHA (with a passphrase of 8 characters or more) and a privacy protocol of AES (with a passphrase of 8 characters or more).
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• Locate the SNMP panel.
• Review the list of configured SNMP Managers and verify that the Version column is set to v3.
• Verify that the Auth Protocol is configured as SHA and the Privacy Protocol is configured as AES.
From the CLI:
• Run the command puresnmp list to display the configuration of the SNMP agent and any SNMP managers.
• Review the output to verify the following for any configured manager or the localhost agent:
• Version is set to v3.
• Auth Protocol is set to SHA.
• Privacy Protocol is set to AES.

Rule.title: Ensure at least 3 NTP servers and an NTP symmetric key are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The network time protocol (NTP) allows time to be synchronized between devices on a network.
Everpure recommends the following:
• Configure at least 3 NTP servers.
• Configure an NTP symmetric key.
Note: The NTP symmetric key cannot be configured through the GUI. This can only be done through the CLI.

Rationale:
There are many security and data protection controls that rely on time. Properly checking the validity of certificates, short lived credentials, and other keys depends on proper time synchronization. Similarly there exist data protection features that rely on time.
As such, synchronization of time on your network is crucial for appropriate security behavior. It is therefore recommended that you configure multiple NTP servers for redundancy.
NTP symmetric keys are used for generating message authentication codes when synchronizing time. These prevent a malicious actor from intercepting and tampering with NTP messages.
FlashArray will ignore NTP messages after initial startup that substantially alter time, but in order to prevent any tampering with time by a bad network actor, Everpure recommends that you configure an NTP symmetric key.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, configure at least three NTP servers and secure the communication using an NTP symmetric key.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the Time panel, locate the NTP Servers section.
• In the New NTP Server(s) text box, type the hostname or IP address of your NTP servers (you can enter multiple servers as comma-separated values).
• Click the Add button. Ensure you have added at least three servers.
From the CLI:
• Configure at least three NTP servers: Specify the servers using the purearray setattr command.
• Command Syntax: purearray setattr --ntpserver <SERVER1>,<SERVER2>,<SERVER3>
• Example: purearray setattr --ntpserver ntp1.example.com,ntp2.example.com,ntp3.example.com
• Configure the NTP symmetric key: Secure the NTP communication by setting a symmetric key using the --ntp-symmetric-key flag. (Note: The key must not contain the " # " character and cannot be longer than 20 characters for an ASCII string or 64 characters for a hex-encoded string).
• Command Syntax: purearray setattr --ntp-symmetric-key <KEY_STRING>

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least three NTP servers are configured for redundancy, and that an NTP symmetric key is configured to prevent tampering with time synchronization.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• Locate the Time panel and review the NTP Servers section.
• Verify that at least three NTP server addresses are listed.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purearray list --ntp.
• Review the output to verify that at least three NTP servers are configured.
• Review the same output to verify that an NTP symmetric key is configured.

Rule.title: Ensure product diagnostic tests for environmental integrations are run periodically
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>For many environmental integrations mentioned in this section, there exists FlashArray functionality to detect that your configuration is still working.
Everpure recommends that you periodically run the product diagnostics tests for the following configurations:
• SAML
• LDAP
• Active Directory
• Syslog
• SMTP Email delivery to alert watchers
• SNMP delivery to SNMP managers
• NTP

Rationale:
Even if a configuration was correct initially, it is possible for it to cease functioning later due to changes in DNS, changes in the network, expiration or rotation of certificates for TLS, removal of credentials, or other similar issues.
Many of these configurations are crucial for security or for monitoring, and so verifying that they are functional ensures non-disrupted product functionality as well as that you will properly be alerted of other system events that may require attention.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, implement an automated script or a manual maintenance schedule to continuously verify that environmental integrations are fully functional.
From the GUI:
• Establish a periodic manual review process to execute available GUI diagnostic tests.
• Test Directory Services: Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
In the Directory Service panel, click Test to verify that URIs resolve and the array can bind to the LDAP/AD tree.
• Test SAML2 SSO: Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies. In the SAML2 SSO pane, click Test (and specifically run the E2E Test) to verify the SP configuration, IdP connectivity, and verification certificate validity.
From the CLI:
• Establish a scheduled process (such as a cron job via the REST API or SSH) to periodically execute the following built-in diagnostic commands:
• SAML2 SSO: puresso saml2 test <IDP-NAME>
• Directory Services: pureds test
• Syslog Servers: purelog syslog test (or purearray test syslogserver)
• SMTP Alert Watchers: purealert watcher test <EMAIL_ADDRESS>
• NTP Servers: purearray test ntp

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that an automated script or regular manual operational process is established to periodically execute product diagnostic tests for SAML, Directory Services (LDAP/AD), Syslog, SMTP Email Delivery, and NTP.
This ensures these integrations have not ceased functioning due to DNS changes, certificate expirations, or network routing issues.
From the GUI:
• Request evidence of a standard operating procedure (SOP) demonstrating that administrators periodically run available connectivity tests.
• Navigate to Settings > Access > Users and Policies.
• In the Directory Service panel, verify that a test is periodically initiated.
• In the SAML2 SSO pane, verify that a test is periodically initiated.
From the CLI:
• Request evidence from your monitoring or automation teams that a script periodically connects to the array to execute configuration test commands (e.g., puresso saml2 test, pureds test, purelog syslog test, purealert watcher test, and purearray test ntp).

Rule.title: Ensure NFS export policies restrict client access and enforce secure authentication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>NFS Export Policies are used to control access to any given file system export over any version of the NFS protocol. They can set properties such as permitted authentication mechanisms, allowance of root access from clients, and read-only vs. read-write based on client network identity.
They may utilize hostnames, IP addresses, subnet ranges, or wildcards as client identities. Any client that does not match any rule in an NFS export policy will be denied access to the exports to which the policy is attached. Everpure recommends the following:
• Do not use wildcard (*) clients in any NFS export policy rules.
• Do not permit sys authentication in any NFS export policy rules.
• Enable root squash for all clients in all NFS export policy rules.
• Constrain the allowed IP addresses to only those clients expected to need access to the exports for any given policy.
• Enable only krb5p authentication for clients where privacy is a concern. krb5i is recommended to be enabled for clients where data integrity is important but data privacy is not.

Rationale:
Use of wildcard clients means that no IP addresses will be denied access to a file system export. Even if using central authentication with kerberos, there is still a risk of some other compromise occurring within the environment. As such, Everpure recommends that you limit the IPs allowed to any access.
krb5p and krb5i both come with performance penalties in order to improve security.
krb5 provides only centralized identity and authentication, but if performance is paramount then it may see use. NFS sys authentication provides no security or identity controls, allowing for clients to act as any user, and should only be considered when there are strong guarantees on network security enforced outside of FlashArray.
However, if such network controls are compromised, sys authentication provides no protection.
Root squash is important to configure in order to avoid privilege escalation on a client, or a rogue client, gaining elevated privileges on the export, as it prevents them from assuming root on the export as a result of having root access locally.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your NFS export policy rules to constrain client IPs, enforce root squash, and require Kerberos security.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Policies.
• In the Export Policies panel, click the name of the NFS policy to modify.
• In the Rules panel, click the + (Create Rule) icon to add a new, secure rule.
(Note: Modifying existing NFS rules via the GUI is done by adding a new rule and removing the non-compliant one).
• Set the Client field to a specific IP subnet (e.g., 192.168.10.0/24).
• Select root-squash for the Access level.
• Select NFSv4 for the Version.
• Select krb5p (or krb5i) for Security, and ensure auth_sys is unchecked.
• Click Create (or Add) to apply the rule.
• Delete the old, overly permissive rule by clicking the trash can (Remove Rule) icon next to it. (Note: Ensure that the User Mapping Enabled toggle is set to true in the policy's Details panel, as this is strictly required for Kerberos authentication).
From the CLI:
• Create a secure rule: Use the purepolicy nfs rule add command to create a rule with explicit client restrictions, root squash, and Kerberos security.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy nfs rule add --client <SUBNET> --root- squash --version nfsv4 --security krb5p <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy nfs rule add --client 192.168.10.0/24 --root- squash --version nfsv4 --security krb5p nfs_secure_policy
• Remove overly permissive rules: Use the purepolicy nfs rule remove command to delete the old, non-compliant rule.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy nfs rule remove --rule-name <RULE_NAME> <POLICY_NAME>
• Apply the policy to an export (if creating a new export): Attach the secure policy to your managed directory using the puredir export create command.
• Command Syntax: puredir export create --dir <FILESYSTEM:DIRECTORY> --policy <POLICY_NAME> <EXPORT_NAME>
• Example: puredir export create --dir FS1:Data --policy nfs_secure_policy DataShare

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that NFS export policies restrict access to specific client IPs (no wildcards), enforce root squashing, and utilize Kerberos ( krb5p or krb5i) for authentication and privacy instead of the default AUTH_SYS.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Policies.
• In the Export Policies panel, click the name of each active NFS policy to view its details.
• Review the Rules panel for the policy and verify the following:
• The Client field specifies explicit IP addresses or subnets (it is not set to * or 0.0.0.0/0).
• The Access field is set to root-squash.
• The Security field is set to krb5p (or krb5i), and auth_sys is not selected.
• The Version field includes nfsv4 (which is required for Kerberos).
From the CLI:
• List all NFS export policies by running the command purepolicy nfs list.
• For each policy, inspect its rules by running the command purepolicy nfs rule list <POLICY_NAME>.
• Review the output to ensure:
• The Client column is restricted to specific subnets or IPs (and does not show *).
• The Access column is set to root-squash.
• The Security column is restricted to krb5p or krb5i (and does not include auth_sys).

Rule.title: Ensure SMB client policies require encryption, restrict client access, and disable anonymous access
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>SMB Client Policies are used to control access to any given file system export over any version of the SMB protocol. They can set properties such as SMB encryption requirements, and read-only vs. read-write based on client network identity.
They may utilize hostnames, IP addresses, subnet ranges, or wildcards as client identities. Any client that does not match any rule in an SMB client policy will be denied access to the exports to which the policy is attached. Everpure recommends the following:
• Do not use wildcard (*) clients in any SMB client policy rules.
• Require SMB encryption in all SMB client policy rules.
• Disable anonymous access in all SMB client policy rules.
• Constrain allowed IPs based on clients' expected to need access to the exports for any given policy.

Rationale:
Use of wildcard clients means that no IP addresses will be denied access to a file system export. Even if using central authentication with kerberos, there is still a risk of some other compromise occurring within the environment. As such, Everpure recommends that you limit the IPs allowed to any access.
SMB encryption ensures privacy and integrity, and is supported by all modern SMB clients. It requires SMB 3.0 or greater.
It does come with additional performance overhead, but it should not be made optional unless configuring clients where performance is paramount, or legacy clients that cannot support modern SMB versions. If it is not configured to be required, Everpure recommends that other controls outside of FlashArray be used to secure the network between FlashArray and its clients.
Anonymous access allows clients to access SMB exports without authentication. It substantially weakens security and can result in unintended information disclosure or tampering. As such it should be disabled.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, update your SMB client policy rules to constrain client IPs, require SMB encryption, and ensure anonymous access remains disabled.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Policies.
• In the Export Policies panel, click the name of the SMB policy to modify.
• In the Rules panel, click the + (Create Rule) icon to add a new, secure rule.
(Note: Modifying existing SMB rules via the GUI is done by adding a new rule and removing the non-compliant one).
• Set the Client field to a specific IP subnet (e.g., 192.168.10.0/24).
• Ensure the SMB Encryption Required toggle is enabled (blue).
• Ensure the Anonymous Access Allowed toggle is disabled (gray).
• Click Create (or Add) to apply the rule.
• Delete the old, overly permissive rule by clicking the trash can (Remove Rule) icon next to it.
From the CLI:
• Create a secure rule: Use the purepolicy smb rule add command to create a rule with explicit client restrictions and required encryption. (Note: Omitting the anonymous access flag restricts anonymous users by default).
• Command Syntax: purepolicy smb rule add --client <SUBNET> --smb- encryption-required <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy smb rule add --client 192.168.10.0/24 --smb- encryption-required smb_secure_policy
• Remove overly permissive rules: Use the purepolicy smb rule remove command to delete the old, non-compliant rule.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy smb rule remove --rule-name <RULE_NAME> <POLICY_NAME>
• Apply the policy to an export (if creating a new export): Attach the secure policy to your managed directory using the puredir export create command.
• Command Syntax: puredir export create --dir <FILESYSTEM:DIRECTORY> --policy <POLICY_NAME> <EXPORT_NAME>
• Example: puredir export create --dir FS1:Data --policy smb_secure_policy DataShare

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that SMB client policies restrict access to specific client IPs (no wildcards), enforce SMB encryption, and restrict anonymous access.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Policies.
• In the Export Policies (or SMB Client Policies) panel, click the name of each active SMB policy to view its details.
• Review the Rules panel for the policy and verify the following:
• The Client field specifies explicit IP addresses or subnets (it is not set to * or 0.0.0.0/0).
• The SMB Encryption Required toggle is enabled (blue).
• The Anonymous Access Allowed toggle is disabled (gray).
From the CLI:
• List all SMB client policies by running the command purepolicy smb list.
• For each policy, inspect its rules by running the command purepolicy smb rule list <POLICY_NAME>.
• Review the output to ensure:
• The Client column is restricted to specific subnets or IPs (and does not show *).
• The SMB Encryption Required attribute is enforced.
• The Anonymous Access Allowed attribute is restricted/disabled.

Rule.title: Ensure native Active Directory integration is used for NFS and SMB identity and authentication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports native integration with Active Directory domains in order to enable LDAP lookups for authorization, and Kerberos authentication, for both NFS and SMB file access.
FlashArray does this by creating a computer account in the domain to represent itself and generate kerberos keys. A unique AD account may be created for each server on the array that needs one.
Everpure recommends that FlashArray's native Active Directory integration be configured in all environments where Active Directory provides identity, authentication, and authorization for NFS and SMB clients.

Rationale:
FlashArray also supports configuring an LDAP directory service, or NIS, for use with NFS for identity and authorization. It also supports manual uploading of kerberos keys to be used for authentication. However, each of these has security weaknesses when compared with native Active Directory integration.
While the LDAP directory service can provide the same level of TLS protection of traffic, its authentication relies on a bind username and password, with simple authentication.
Comparatively, native Active Directory integration allows the array to represent itself with a computer account and authenticate to the domain using kerberos. No raw passwords are ever stored on the array. This allows for stronger authentication and identity.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, join the FlashArray file server to your Active Directory domain.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Servers and click your file server to access its settings.
• In the Remote Directory Service panel, click the Edit Configuration icon to the right and select Active Directory.
• In the Configure Remote Directory Service window, enter a Name, the Domain DNS Name, and the Computer Name for the array.
• Enter the AD User and AD Password for an Active Directory account with permission to create a new computer account (or select the Use Existing Account toggle if pre-created by your AD admin).
• Ensure TLS Mode is set to required.
• Click Create to apply the configuration and join the domain.
From the CLI:
• Join the file server to Active Directory using the puread account create command.
• Command Syntax: puread account create --domain <DOMAIN> -- computer-name <COMPUTER_NAME> <NAME>
• Example: puread account create --domain sales.local --computer- name SalesDocs server1::SalesAD (Note: The CLI will prompt interactively for the Active Directory administrator credentials to perform the join; Purity//FA does not store these credentials).
• Verify the configuration by running the puread account list command.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that FlashArray file services are natively integrated with an Active Directory domain to enable secure Kerberos authentication and strong identity authorization for SMB and NFS clients.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Servers and click the name of your file server.
• Locate the Remote Directory Service panel.
• Verify that the Active Directory configuration is present and actively displays the correct domain and computer name.
From the CLI:
• Check the Active Directory domain join status by running the command puread account list.
• Review the output to verify that your file server's AD account is listed and the Domain field is correct.

Rule.title: Ensure a hard-limit quota policy is enforced on the root managed directory of every file system
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports configuring quota policies in order to enforce space consumption limits on directories. These allow you to limit the total amount of space any directory and its child files and directories can consume.
Quota policies can be configured to use a soft limit, meaning they only alert when space exceeds the limit, or enforce a hard limit, meaning that new writes to the directory will be blocked when it is detected that the limit has been exceeded.
Everpure recommends that you configure a quota policy that enforces a hard limit on the root managed directory for every file system.

Rationale:
When strong security is configured to prevent malicious destruction of data, it also creates the risk that a malicious actor can write junk data to fill up a storage array, causing a system-wide outage.
• Enforcing space limits ensures that even if a malicious actor gains access to one directory, they cannot consume all the space on the system.
• Enforcing a space limit on the root directory of every file system ensures that, regardless of configurations and exports of sub-directories, that file system will not be able to consume all of the space on the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, create a quota policy with an enforced hard limit and attach it to the root managed directory of each file system.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Policies.
• In the Quota Policies panel, click the + (Create Policy) icon.
• In the pop-up window, enter a Name for the policy.
• In the rules section, specify the Quota Limit (e.g., 5T).
• Click the Enabled toggle icon next to Enforced so that it turns blue. This ensures new writes are blocked when the limit is exceeded. Click Create.
• Click the name of your newly created quota policy.
• In the Members panel, click the menu icon and select Add Member.
• Select the root directory (e.g., fs1:root) of your file system and click Add to apply the policy.
From the CLI:
• Create the quota policy:
• Command Syntax: purepolicy quota create <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy quota create root_hard_quota
• Add an enforced rule to the policy: Add a rule with your desired size limit and ensure the --enforced flag is used.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy quota rule add --quota-limit <SIZE> -- enforced <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy quota rule add --quota-limit 5T --enforced root_hard_quota
• Attach the policy to the root directory: Apply the policy to the root managed directory of your file system.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy quota add --dir <FILESYSTEM>:root <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy quota add --dir FS1:root root_hard_quota

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that an enforced (hard limit) directory quota policy is actively configured and applied to the root managed directory of every file system. This ensures that no single file system can be maliciously filled to consume the entire storage array.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Storage > Policies and locate the Quota Policies panel.
• Click the name of a quota policy and review the Rules panel to ensure the Enforced attribute is active (which creates a hard limit rather than a soft notification).
• Navigate to Storage > File Systems and select your file system.
• Locate the Directory Quotas panel. Verify that a quota policy with an enforced hard limit is attached to the root managed directory (e.g., fs1:root).
From the CLI:
• Run the command puredir quota list to display all directories with an attached quota policy. Verify that the root managed directories for your file systems are listed.
• Run the command purepolicy quota rule list to inspect the rules for the attached policies. Verify that the Enforced column is set to True and an appropriate Quota Limit is established.

Rule.title: Ensure space consumption and performance are monitored for anomalies
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray offers capabilities for monitoring space consumption, data reduction, and performance across a variety of axes.
For performance, these include, but are not limited to:
• Array-wide
• By directory
• By volume
• By volume group
• By host
• By host group For space, these include, but are not limited to:
• Array-wide
• By directory
• By volume
• By volume group
• By host
• By host group Everpure recommends the following:
• Monitor the space consumption at various levels over time for anomalies such as rapid reduction in space utilization or data reduction.
• Monitor performance at various levels over time for anomalies such as spikes in reads or writes by a specific client or user.

Rationale:
Sudden trends resulting in reduction in the data reduction ratio can indicate potential Ransomware attacks. Rapid reductions in utilized space can indicate malicious deletion of data.
An unexpected spike in read bandwidth by a specific client, when compared to space utilization, can indicate potential exfiltration of data.
Other similar anomalies in space and performance monitoring can indicate rogue actors having gained access to some part of the storage system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, implement a regular monitoring process using the built-in Analysis dashboards or automated CLI scripts to track capacity and performance trends.
From the GUI:
• Establish a continuous manual monitoring routine using the Analysis > Capacity and Analysis > Performance pages to monitor capacity trends and bandwidth/IOPS metrics.
• Ensure you have configured syslog servers or email alert watchers (as covered in earlier sections) so that built-in capacity alerts (e.g., warnings when storage consumption reaches 90% of usable capacity) are proactively pushed to your monitoring teams.
From the CLI:
• Implement a scheduled automation script to periodically pull space and performance metrics to an external monitoring system using the following commands:
• Array Space: purearray list --space
• Array Performance: purearray monitor
• File System / Directory Space: puredir list --space

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that space consumption and I/O performance are continuously monitored at the array, file system, and directory levels to detect potential anomalies such as ransomware encryption, data exfiltration, or malicious deletion.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Analysis > Performance to review the array-wide and volume-level I/O metrics (Latency, IOPS, and Bandwidth) for any unexpected spikes or anomalies.
• Navigate to Analysis > Capacity to review current array capacity utilization and trends.
• Navigate to Storage > File Systems to verify the capacity utilization of specific file systems.
From the CLI:
• Check file system / directory space usage by running the command puredir list --space.
• Check real-time or historical array performance metrics by running the command purearray monitor (or purearray monitor --historical <TIME>).
• Check array-wide space usage by running the command purearray list -- space.

Rule.title: Ensure SMB audit policies with syslog and file log targets are attached to production file systems
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports creation of one or more audit policies for enabling audit of operations over the SMB data protocol.
These audit policies may be used to send audit records to remote syslog servers for monitoring. Everpure recommends the following:
• Configure at least 1 syslog server and 1 directory as log targets among your audit policies for SMB.
• Configure at least 1 audit policy with a syslog log target, attached to each file system that stores production data and enables the SMB protocol for access.
• Configure at least 1 audit policy with a file log target, attached to each file system that stores production data and enables the SMB protocol for access.
• Instruct administrative users for each file system SMB export to configure appropriate SACLs to ensure proper auditing.

Rationale:
Auditing access and operations to file data over the SMB protocol allows for detection of unexpected behavior by SMB clients, which can indicate malicious actors gaining unintended access to an export.
Sending of audit records to a remote syslog server allows for logs across systems to be aggregated and analyzed centrally. This allows for better analysis of patterns spanning across systems and management of retention for detection and response, but it can also lead to dropped logs due to network bandwidth limitations.
Locally stored audit records do not have a dependency on the network, and can be more reliable, but can be more difficult to integrate into real-time analysis pipelines since they would need to be periodically pulled.
As such, it is recommended that both remote syslog and local log targets be utilized, with appropriate retention based on your environment. This enables central aggregation of audit records for detection and response, while also ensuring that there is a robust local backup of logs in case of a network or syslog server outage.
Which files, directories, and operations within a file system are audited is determined by SACLs, and which users can set SACLs is determined by the GPOs in your Active Directory domain. So users in the appropriate groups must be instructed to configure SACLs appropriately in order to ensure auditing is enabled.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, establish file log targets, create an audit policy, attach it to your production managed directories, and externally configure SACLs for SMB exports.
From the GUI:
• Create the File Log Target: Navigate to Settings > System. In the File Log Targets panel, click the + (Create) icon. Provide a name, select an empty managed directory to store the logs, configure a retention policy (Keep For or Keep Size), and click Create.
• Create the Syslog Target (if not already configured): In the Syslog Servers panel, add your remote syslog server URI.
• Create the Audit Policy: Navigate to Storage > Policies. In the Audit Policies panel, click the + (Create Policy) icon. Provide a name, ensure the Enabled toggle is active, select the File Log Target and Syslog Target you created in the Log Targets prompt, and click Create.
• Attach the Policy to Directories: Click your newly created audit policy to open it. In the Members panel, click the menu icon, select Add member..., select your production managed directories, and click Add.
• Configure SACLs: Instruct your file server administrators to connect to the SMB export using a Windows client and utilize Windows MMC to configure the SACLs that dictate which file operations generate audit events.
From the CLI:
• Create Log Targets:
• Command Syntax: purelog file create --dir <FILESYSTEM:DIRECTORY> - -keep-for <PERIOD> <NAME>
• Command Syntax: purelog syslog create --uri tls://<HOST>:<PORT> <SYSLOG_NAME>
• Create the Audit Policy:
• Command Syntax: purepolicy audit file create --targets <TARGET1>,<TARGET2> <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy audit file create --targets local_dir_target,syslog_target smb_audit_policy
• Attach to Directories:
• Command Syntax: purepolicy audit file add --dir <FILESYSTEM:DIRECTORY> <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy audit file add --dir FS1:Data smb_audit_policy
• Enable the Policy:
• Command Syntax: purepolicy audit file enable <POLICY_NAME>
• Configure SACLs: Establish appropriate SACLs externally using Windows MMC.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least one syslog server and one local directory are configured as file log targets, and that an active audit policy is attached to all file systems utilizing SMB.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System to verify that a remote syslog server is configured (in the Syslog Servers panel) and a local directory is configured (in the File Log Targets panel).
• Navigate to Storage > Policies.
• Scroll to the Audit Policies panel and select your configured audit policy.
• Review the Details panel to verify that both the local directory and syslog server are listed as log targets.
• Review the Members panel to verify that the policy is attached to the appropriate production managed directories. (Note: Verifying that proper System Access Control Lists (SACLs) are applied to the SMB share must be done externally via Windows MMC or similar tools, as this is not visible in the Purity GUI).
From the CLI:
• Run the commands purelog file list and purelog syslog list to verify that local and remote log targets exist.
• Run the command purepolicy audit file list to verify that an audit policy exists and its Enabled status is set to True.
• Review the policy members by running purepolicy audit file list --member to ensure the policies are successfully attached to the correct source managed directories.

Rule.title: Ensure manual eradication is disabled and the eradication delay is at least 8 days for production data
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray possesses a variety of configurations, such as realms and pods, that pertain to data protection.
These configurations can have their data eradication properties configured. Everpure recommends the following:
• Disable manual eradication for all pods, realms, or arrays that will contain production data.
• Set the eradication delay for objects that cannot be manually eradicated to be at least 8 days.

Rationale:
In case of administrative compromise, it is important to safeguard against manual erasure of all system data and backups.
Disabling manual eradication of important data is a crucial step towards preventing such compromise.
For containers such as pods, disabling manual eradication prevents its contents from being manually eradicated.
When manual eradication is disabled for a pgroup, both the volumes and snapshots associated with that pgroup will not be able to be manually eradicated.
When manual eradication of an object is disabled, it may be destroyed (i.e. put into the recycling bin), but will not be able to be eradicated and fully erased until the configured eradication delay has elapsed. It is important to ensure that this delay is reasonably long to prevent quick deletion of data on a compromised system.
Separate delays can be configured for objects that can be manually eradicated and those that cannot; ensuring that those that cannot be manually eradicated have a delay of at least 8 days ensures a reasonable window of protection.
This eradication delay is measured in system uptime, not wall time. As such, this eradication delay is resistant to attempts at NTP tampering.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, extend the disabled eradication delay to at least 8 days and engage SafeMode retention locks to disable manual eradication.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• In the Eradication Configuration panel, click the edit icon in the upper right corner.
• Set the Disabled Delay to at least 8 days (14 days is mathematically recommended to provide a 2-week buffer).
• Click Save.
• To actively disable manual eradication, you must enable SafeMode retention locks on your data. Navigate to Protection > Protection Groups, click the name of your protection group to open its details, and in the SafeMode pane, click the edit icon to ratchet the retention lock. (Note: Array-wide SafeMode enrollment requires contacting Everpure Technical Services with at least two administrators and PIN codes).
From the CLI:
• Set the Eradication Delay: Configure the disabled delay using the purearray eradication-config setattr command.
• Command Syntax: purearray eradication-config setattr --disabled- delay <DAYS>d
• Example: purearray eradication-config setattr --disabled-delay 14d
• Disable Manual Eradication: Enforce manual eradication prevention by ratcheting the SafeMode retention lock on your protection groups using the purepgroup retention-lock ratchet command.
• Command Syntax: purepgroup retention-lock ratchet <PGROUP>
• Example: purepgroup retention-lock ratchet pgroup1

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that the manual eradication of data is disabled (via SafeMode) and that the eradication delay for protected objects is set to a minimum of 8 days.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Settings > System.
• Locate the Eradication Configuration panel.
• Verify that the Disabled Delay is set to at least 8 days (or higher).
• Verify that the Manual Eradication column does not read all-enabled (it should read all-disabled or partially-disabled to indicate SafeMode is actively protecting objects from being manually destroyed).
From the CLI:
• Run the command purearray eradication-config list to view the eradication delay values and manual eradication status.
• Review the output to ensure the Disabled Delay is at least 8d and the Manual Eradication status is not all-enabled.

Rule.title: Ensure production volumes and hosts are protected by ratcheted (SafeMode) protection groups with daily snapshots
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows for protection groups (pgroups) to be created. These pgroups can be attached to hosts and volumes in order to schedule the creation and replication of snapshots for the purpose of data protection.
Additionally, pgroups may be ratcheted to enable a feature known as SafeMode. Once a pgroup has its retention lock set to ratcheted, the protection that it provides can only be increased, not decreased. So it may be attached to more things, and made to make more snapshots; but it cannot be detached from its members or changed to take and retain fewer snapshots.
Administrators of the array will not be able to un-ratchet the retention lock and reduce protection without involving Everpure Support. Everpure recommends the following:
• Associate all volumes with at least one pgroup, or add them to a volume group with an associated pgroup.
• Associate all hosts with at least one pgroup, or add them to a host group with an associated pgroup.
• Ratchet all pgroups that will be associated with production data, in order to disable manual eradication of the associated data.
• Configure pgroups to create at least 1 snapshot per day.
• Configure pgroups to replicate at least 1 snapshot per day.
• Configure pgroups to retain each snapshot for at least 7 days.

Rationale:
Automatically, periodically creating immutable backups is an important aspect of data protection. Because FlashArray snapshot contents are immutable, they cannot be targeted for encryption by threats such as Ransomware.
Ratcheting the pgroup ensures that protection cannot be reduced in the case of administrative compromise, and disabling manual eradication prevents data erasure by a compromised administrator.
• In order to mitigate the impact of an attack on any host or volume, every host or volume on a FlashArray should have at least one pgroup automating the creation of backups, either directly or indirectly via a group.
• In order to mitigate the impact of a physical system being destroyed or tampered with, replicating backups automatically is highly recommended.
Snapshots can be used to restore the prior state of a volume that has been tampered with, and so it is recommended that at least 1 snapshot be taken daily. Because it may take some time to discover tampering, it is recommended that they be retained for at least 7 days.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, create a volume-based protection group, establish daily snapshot and replication schedules with at least 7 days of retention, and ratchet the group to enable SafeMode.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Protection Groups.
• In the Source Protection Groups panel, click the + (Create Protection Group) icon, enter a name, and click Create.
• Click on the newly created protection group to open its details.
• In the Members pane, click the menu icon, select Add..., select your production volumes, and click Add.
• In the Snapshot Schedule and Replication Schedule panes, click the Edit (pen and paper) icon. Toggle the schedule to Enabled (blue), configure it to create/replicate a snapshot at least every 1 days (or more frequent), and configure the retention to retain snapshots for at least 7 days. Click Save.
• In the SafeMode pane, click the edit icon and click the Ratcheted toggle button to enable (blue) the SafeMode feature. (Note: Once ratcheted, a protection group cannot be unlocked without explicit authorization and intervention from Everpure Technical Services).
From the CLI:
• Create the protection group:
• Command Syntax: purepgroup create <PGROUP>
• Add volume members:
• Command Syntax: purevol add --pgroup <PGROUP> <VOLUMES>
• Configure the schedules (at least daily):
• Command Syntax: purepgroup schedule --snap-frequency 1d -- replicate-frequency 1d <PGROUP>
• Configure the retention (at least 7 days):
• Command Syntax: purepgroup retain --all-for 1d --per-day 1 --days 7 <PGROUP>
• Enable the schedules:
• Command Syntax: purepgroup enable <PGROUP>
• Ratchet the protection group to enable SafeMode:
• Command Syntax: purepgroup retention-lock ratchet <PGROUP>

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that production volumes are protected by a protection group, that the protection group enforces SafeMode (ratcheted), and that snapshots are scheduled at least daily and retained for a minimum of 7 days. (Note: SafeMode retention lock cannot be enabled on protection groups containing hosts, host groups, or offload targets; you must explicitly target the underlying volumes).
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Protection Groups.
• Click on a source protection group to view its details.
• Review the Members pane to verify that production volumes are included (and ensure no hosts, host groups, or offload targets are included).
• Review the SafeMode pane and verify that the Retention Lock status is set to ratcheted.
• Review the Snapshot Schedule and Replication Schedule panes to verify that they are enabled, configured to run at least once every 24 hours (1 day), and that the retention strategy keeps snapshots for at least 7 days.
From the CLI:
• Run the commands purevol list --protect (and purehost list --protect) to verify that your production workloads are actively associated with a protection group.
• Run the command purepgroup list --retention-lock to verify the SafeMode status is ratcheted for your production protection groups.
• Run the commands purepgroup list --schedule and purepgroup list -- retention to verify that the snapshot and replication frequencies are at least daily and retained for at least 7 days.

Rule.title: Ensure an enabled snapshot policy taking at least one daily snapshot is attached to every directory
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray supports creating snapshot policies for automatically creating, managing, and deleting immutable snapshots of FlashArray directories. These policies can be additionally used to replicate file snapshots.
Everpure recommends the following if you have any file systems on the system:
• Attach at least one enabled snapshot policy to each directory.
• Configure snapshot policies to create at least 1 snapshot per day.
• Configure snapshot policies to retain each snapshot for at least 7 days.

Rationale:
Automatically, periodically creating immutable backups is an important aspect of data protection. Because FlashArray snapshot contents are immutable, they cannot be targeted for encryption by threats such as Ransomware.
In order to mitigate the impact of an attack on any export, every file system on a FlashArray should have at least one snapshot policy.
Snapshots can be used to restore the prior state of a file system that has been tampered with. Everpure recommends that at least 1 snapshot be taken daily and because it may take some time to discover tampering, that the snapshots be retained for at least 7 days.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, establish a snapshot policy that takes daily snapshots with a 7-day retention period, and attach it to your file system managed directories.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Policies.
• In the Snapshot Policies panel, click the + (Create Policy) icon. Provide a name, ensure the Enabled toggle is active (blue), and click Create.
• Click on the newly created policy name to open its details.
• In the Rules panel, click the + (Create Rule) icon (or menu icon > Create...) to add a new rule.
• Set Create 1 snapshot every to 1d (or a shorter interval like 12h).
• Set And keep for to 1w (or 7d or a longer duration like 30d).
• Provide a Client Name (e.g., daily) which will be visible to users recovering files, then click Add.
• In the Members panel, click the menu icon, select Add Member..., select your managed directories, and click Add to attach the policy.
From the CLI:
• Create the Policy: Create a new snapshot policy using the purepolicy snapshot create command.
• Command Syntax: purepolicy snapshot create <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy snapshot create data_snap
• Add a Compliant Rule: Add a rule configuring the frequency (--every), retention (--keep-for), and client name (--client-name).
• Command Syntax: purepolicy snapshot rule add --every <FREQUENCY> - -keep-for <RETENTION> --client-name <NAME> <POLICY_NAME>
• Example: purepolicy snapshot rule add --every 1d --keep-for 7d -- client-name daily data_snap
• Attach to Directories: Attach the policy to your file system directories using the puredir snapshot add command.
• Command Syntax: puredir snapshot add --policy <POLICY_NAME> <FILESYSTEM:DIRECTORY>
• Example: puredir snapshot add --policy data_snap FS1:Data

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that an active snapshot policy is attached to your production directories, ensuring that immutable snapshots are taken at least daily and retained for a minimum of 7 days to protect against ransomware and accidental deletion.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Policies.
• In the Snapshot Policies panel, verify that a snapshot policy exists and its Enabled status is set to true.
• Click the name of the policy to view its details.
• Review the Rules panel and verify that the Create 1 snapshot every frequency is 1d (or more frequent) and the And keep for retention period is at least 7d (or 1w or longer).
• Review the Members panel to verify that all production directories are listed and actively attached to the policy.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purepolicy snapshot rule list to verify the configured rules on your snapshot policies.
• Review the output to ensure the frequency (every) is at least daily (1d) and the retention (keep_for) is at least 7 days (7d or 1w).
• Run the command purepolicy snapshot list --member to view all configured snapshot policies and verify that your production managed directories are successfully attached to them.

Rule.title: Ensure default protection is configured at the array level and for every pod
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows the array and its pods to have default protection configured.
This allows you to configure pgroups that will be automatically associated with any volumes created within the pod or the array. This can be used to ensure that all block data has some level of data protection by default.
Everpure recommends the following if you intend to place any volumes on the system:
• Configure at least 1 pgroup as the default protection for every pod on the system, and at the array level.
• Any pgroups configured as default protection for containers that will have production data should have a ratcheted retention lock, with manual eradication disabled.

Rationale:
In case of administrative compromise, it is important to safeguard against manual erasure of all system data and backups.
Default protection ensures that you do not need to take extra steps to achieve a baseline protection of block data. It reduces the risk of user error causing a lapse in data protection.
It is also important to ensure that the default protection is reasonably strong, which is why it is recommended to ratchet the default protection for any production data, ensuring that it cannot be weakened and it disables manual eradication of the protected data.
When manual eradication of file is disabled, file systems and snapshots may be destroyed (i.e. put into the recycling bin), but will not be able to be eradicated and fully erased until the configured eradication delay has elapsed. This applies to all snapshots, not just those created by the safemode policy.
This eradication delay is measured in system uptime, not wall time. As such, this eradication delay is resistant to attempts at NTP tampering.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, assign a ratcheted protection group to the array root and all pods so that newly provisioned data receives baseline SafeMode protection automatically.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• In the Default Protection panel, click the Edit (Set Default Protection) icon on the right of the appropriate row (the - row for the root of the array, or the row for a specific pod).
• In the Available Protection Groups column, select the protection groups to be added so they appear in the Selected Protection Groups column.
• Click Set.
• Navigate to Protection > Protection Groups and select your assigned default protection group.
• In the SafeMode pane, if the status is unlocked, click the edit icon and toggle the Ratcheted button to enabled (blue).
From the CLI:
• Set the Default Protection List: Define the default protection groups for the array root or a pod using the purearray default-protection set command.
• Command Syntax (Array Root): purearray default-protection set -- pgroup <PGROUP> ""
• Command Syntax (Pod): purearray default-protection set --pgroup <POD>::<PGROUP> <POD>
• Example: purearray default-protection set --pgroup pod1::pg1 pod1
• Ratchet the Protection Group: Ensure SafeMode is enabled on the default protection group to prevent manual eradication.
• Command Syntax: purepgroup retention-lock ratchet <PGROUP>

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least one protection group is configured as the default protection for every pod and the array root, and that they enforce SafeMode (ratcheted) to prevent manual eradication of newly provisioned volumes.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• Scroll to the Default Protection panel.
• Verify that a protection group is listed for the array root (denoted by - in the Container Name column) and for every configured pod.
• Navigate to Protection > Protection Groups.
• Click on the protection groups listed as defaults to view their details.
• In the SafeMode pane, verify that the Retention Lock status is set to ratcheted.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purearray default-protection list to view the default protection group lists for the array root (denoted by - in the Container Name column) and all pods.
• Run the command purepgroup list --retention-lock to verify that the SafeMode status is ratcheted and manual eradication is disabled for the protection groups assigned as defaults.

Rule.title: Ensure at least one encrypted array connection is configured for replication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows for connections to be created between any 2 FlashArrays for the purpose of replicating block and file data asynchronously, or block data synchronously.
This allows for backups of data to be copied to other arrays, enabling disaster recovery.
FlashArray supports creating pods and using them to store file and block data to coordinate replication. Everpure recommends the following:
• Create at least one array connection.
• Encrypt all array connections.
• Ensure all peer arrays are on at least the same minor version, if not the same patch version.
• Add all file systems and directories to a pod with at least one replica link for backing up data.
• Add all volumes to either a pgroup with a replication schedule, a pod with at least one replica link for backing up data, or a stretched pod.

Rationale:
Backing up data to a secondary system is important for recovery in the case of disasters, as well as physical compromise that may render an array unusable. As such, Everpure recommends that there be at least one array peer utilized for backups.
Encrypting backup traffic in flight is crucial for ensuring backups of block and file data cannot be tampered with or have any sensitive contents exposed. Trust and privacy is established using TLS pre-shared keys with TLS1.3 in order to prevent interception of traffic.
While FlashArray does support replication between peers of different versions, some security features may only be available or effective when both arrays in an array connection are sufficiently new in version. Everpure recommends the following:
• Both arrays should be on 6.9.x. Ideally both are on the latest version of 6.9.x, or very close versions.
• All data on the array have at least one backup destination, regardless of whether it is file or block data.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, establish an encrypted array connection using an encrypted pre-shared key, and ensure your production data is actively replicating.
From the GUI:
• Get the Connection Key: Log in to the target array, navigate to Protection > Array, click the menu icon in the Connected Arrays panel, and select Create Encrypted Connection Key. Copy the key.
• Connect the Arrays: Log in to the source array, navigate to Protection > Array, click the menu icon in the Connected Arrays panel, and select Connect Array.
• Enter the target array's Management Address, select the Type (Async or Sync Replication), provide the Encrypted Connection Key, ensure Replication Transport is set to Ethernet (IP), and toggle Encrypted to enabled (blue). Click Connect.
• (Optional - Encrypt an Existing Connection): Click the menu icon for an existing connection and select Edit Connected Array, toggle Encrypted to enabled (blue), and click Save. You will be required to provide a newly generated encrypted connection key from the target array.
• Protect the Data: Navigate to Storage > Volumes or Storage > File Systems and assign your data to a pod or protection group configured for replication.
From the CLI:
• Get the Encrypted Key: On the target array, run the command purearray list -- connection-key --encrypted to generate a one-time-use encrypted pre-shared key.
• Connect the Arrays: On the source array, run the purearray connect command with the --encrypted flag.
• Command Syntax: purearray connect --management-address <IP_OR_FQDN> --type <async-replication|sync-replication> -- encrypted
• Action: Purity will prompt you interactively to paste the encrypted connection key.
• Encrypt an Existing Connection: If an unencrypted connection already exists, you can secure it using the purearray connection enable command.
• Command Syntax: purearray connection enable --encrypted <ARRAY_NAME>
• Action: Purity will prompt you interactively to paste a newly generated encrypted connection key from the target array.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that at least one array connection exists for backups, that the replication transport utilizes Ethernet (IP) with encryption enabled, and that production volumes and file systems are assigned to a replicating pod or protection group.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• In the Connected Arrays panel, verify that at least one remote array is listed and connected.
• Review the connection details in the panel and verify that the connection uses an Ethernet (IP) Replication Transport and that Encryption is enabled (or check the Encrypted toggle by clicking the menu icon and selecting Edit Connected Array).
• Navigate to Storage > Volumes and Storage > File Systems. Verify that the production objects belong to a Pod (that is stretched or has an ActiveDR replica link) or a Protection Group (with a replication schedule actively sending data to a target array).
From the CLI:
• Run the command purearray connection list to view the status and attributes of connected arrays.
• Review the output to ensure that a connection exists, the Transport is ip, and Encryption is set to encrypted.
• Run the purevol list --protect and purefs list commands to verify that all storage objects are associated with a replicating protection group or pod.

Rule.title: Ensure a snapshot offload target using HTTPS is configured when no array connection is available
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>FlashArray allows for connections to be created between a FlashArray and a generic offload target.
Offload targets allow snapshots to be stored externally to the array, with storage and transmission of proprietary-format snapshots via standardized 3rd party protocols.
Offload targets can either utilize the S3 data format, such as Amazon AWS, or the Azure blob format. This allows for backups of data to be copied to a 3rd party backup target, enabling disaster recovery.
This can be an alternative to array connections for backups if there is no secondary FlashArray available.
If no array connection can be created, Everpure recommends that you configure at least one offload target.
If an offload target is created, and a URI or endpoint is specified, Everpure recommends that it utilizes https.

Rationale:
Backing up data to a secondary system is important for recovery in the case of disasters, as well as physical compromise that may render an array unusable.
If backup to a secondary FlashArray is unavailable, backup to a 3rd party storage provider can be a reasonable alternative. Such backups should still be encrypted using https.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
To align with the security recommendations, establish an offload target to act as a secondary backup repository and ensure secure transmission by enforcing HTTPS for any custom endpoints.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• In the Offload Targets panel, click the + (connect) icon.
• In the Connect Offload Target window, select the Protocol (s3 or azure).
• For Azure Blob: Type a target Name, the Microsoft Azure Account name, the Container name, and the Secret Access Key.
• For S3: Type a target Name, the AWS Access Key ID, the Bucket name, and the Secret Access Key.
• If a custom endpoint/URI is required, ensure it begins with https://.
• If this is the first time a FlashArray is connecting to this specific bucket or container and it is currently empty, select the check box to Initialize the target.
• Click Connect.
From the CLI:
• Connect to Azure Blob: Connect the array to a Microsoft Azure Blob container using the pureoffload azure connect command. (Note: Purity//FA will prompt you interactively to enter the secret access key twice).
• Command Syntax: pureoffload azure connect --account-name <ACCOUNT> --container-name <CONTAINER> <TARGET_NAME>
• Connect to S3: Connect the array to an S3 bucket using the pureoffload s3 connect command. If using a custom URI, enforce HTTPS using the --uri flag.
(Note: Purity//FA will prompt you interactively to enter the secret access key twice).
• Command Syntax: pureoffload s3 connect --access-key-id <KEY_ID> -- bucket <BUCKET> --uri https://<URI> <TARGET_NAME>
• Initialize the target (Optional): Append the --initialize flag to either command if this is the first time the array is connecting to the empty Azure container or S3 bucket.

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that if an array connection cannot be created for replication, at least one snapshot offload target is configured, and that any custom URIs specified for the target strictly utilize HTTPS to encrypt data in flight.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• Scroll to the Offload Targets panel and verify that at least one target is listed and its Status is connected.
• Review the Details column to verify that if a custom URI/endpoint is configured, it utilizes https://.
From the CLI:
• Run the command pureoffload list to display all connected offload targets and their general statuses.
• Run pureoffload s3 list or pureoffload azure list to display detailed connection settings.
• Review the output to ensure the connection exists and that any defined URI uses the https:// protocol rather than http://.

Rule.title: Ensure the health of array connections and offload targets is continuously monitored
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Whether utilizing array connections or offload targets, FlashArray periodically monitors them for health issues that impact your ability to backup data.
Everpure recommends that you monitor the health of your array connections and offload targets, in order to detect unhealthy statuses.

Rationale:
Replication backups are crucial for security, and so verifying that replication connections are functional ensures non-disrupted data protection functionality.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Because this is a continuous monitoring procedure, remediation involves establishing regular manual or automated review processes to track connection metrics and respond to anomalies.
From the GUI (for manual monitoring):
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• In the Connected Arrays panel, monitor the Status column. A status of connecting indicates an unhealthy connection (typically due to network issues), while quarantined indicates an unstable synchronous replication path that has been temporarily embargoed.
• In the Offload Targets panel, monitor the Status column. A status of connecting indicates an unhealthy network connection to the bucket/container, while Not Connected indicates the offload app itself is not running.
• Navigate to Health > Alerts to proactively review any generated alerts citing degraded connections or unhealthy paths.
From the CLI (for manual monitoring or scripted checks): Establish a scheduled process (such as a cron job via REST API or SSH) to periodically execute the following diagnostic commands:
• Monitor Array Connections: Run purearray connection list periodically.
Investigate any paths that do not report a connected status.
• Monitor Offload Targets: Run pureoffload list periodically to ensure external storage targets are successfully reachable.
• Monitor ActiveDR/ActiveCluster: Run purepod replica-link list to check for unhealthy ActiveDR links, and purepod list --mediator to ensure the Pure1 Cloud Mediator is Online and not Unreachable.
• Monitor Alerts: Run purealert list to view recent system alerts regarding connectivity drops. (Note: The puremessage command was deprecated in Purity//FA 6.8.0 and its functionality is now handled by purealert).

check.check-content:
To align with the security recommendations, verify that array connections, offload targets, and replication links are actively monitored to ensure they are healthy and fully functioning.
From the GUI:
• Navigate to Protection > Array.
• Review the Connected Arrays panel and verify that the Status column for peer arrays shows as connected rather than connecting or quarantined.
• Review the Offload Targets panel and verify that the Status column shows as connected rather than connecting, Scanning, or Not Connected.
• Navigate to Protection > ActiveDR and review the Replica Links pane to ensure no links display an unhealthy status.
From the CLI:
• Run the command purearray connection list to verify the status of peer array connections.
• Run the command purepod replica-link list to verify the status of ActiveDR connections.
• Run the command pureoffload list to display all connected offload targets.
• Review the outputs to ensure the paths are healthy and not displaying a connecting, quarantined, or unhealthy state.
